ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy can reconstruct neural circuits, but for half a century the images were analyzed largely by hand. Machine-learning methods that learn image features from examples now offer a path to automate that tracing at the scale of cubic-millimeter brain volumes.
ocar.challenge: Earlier automation attempts never fully replaced manual labor. Convolutional nets can find neuronal boundaries accurately on clean images, yet real serial-section data contain defects, and the same tools must also find synapses, identify synaptic partners, edit reconstructions, and align sections into a 3D stack. Computational systems must handle petavoxel images.
ocar.action: Lee, Turner, Macrina, Wu, Lu, and Seung review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019) how convolutional nets are applied across the serial-section EM reconstruction pipeline, from boundary detection to synapse finding, reconstruction editing, and serial-section alignment, including systems aimed at cubic-millimeter mouse volumes such as those associated with MICrONS.
ocar.resolution: The review reports that convolutional nets have reached impressive accuracy on clean images and are now used for multiple reconstruction tasks, while engineering effort is focused on petavoxel-scale processing.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag robust handling of image defects as a major outstanding challenge, and imply that scaling these nets to defective, cubic-millimeter serial-section volumes remains the next hurdle.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can photograph brain tissue in extremely thin slices and try to follow every wire. This review explains how computers that learn from example images are starting to do that tracing automatically, though messy photos remain hard.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Lee, Turner, Macrina, Wu, Lu, and Seung survey convolutional networks for reconstructing circuits from serial-section electron microscopy. They note that nets first applied to neuronal boundary detection about a dozen years earlier now perform well on clean images, and are also used to find synapses and partners, extend or prune reconstructions, and align sections. The review emphasizes engineering for petavoxel, cubic-millimeter volumes, with mouse serial-section EM as the motivating setting.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review, not a new benchmark. The claim of impressive accuracy is explicitly restricted to clean images; the authors themselves treat defect robustness as unsolved. Pipeline coverage is broad (boundaries, synapses, partners, editing, alignment) but quantitative comparisons across tasks are not given in the abstract. Scaling claims concern systems being engineered for petavoxel data rather than a completed cubic-millimeter reconstruction in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can photograph brain tissue in extremely thin slices and try to follow every wire. This review explains how computers that learn from example images are starting to do that tracing automatically, though messy photos remain hard.

ocar.opportunity: As electron-microscopy connectomic datasets grow, the field needs more than a frozen snapshot at publication: collaborators should be able to branch, edit, and reintegrate reconstructions the way software communities use version control.
ocar.challenge: Publishing only a static copy of a huge EM volume makes it hard for remote groups to try new segmentations or proofreading and then merge accepted changes back. Storage backends also differ, from laptops to cloud object stores, so a single dataservice must remain efficient across data types and hardware.
ocar.action: Katz and Plaza introduce DVID in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2019): an open-source, web-based connectomics API with distributed versioning, used as the central data resource for Janelia’s FlyEM team. It supports branched, versioned data for proofreader training and segmentation experiments, and can persist to local SSDs or cloud stores.
ocar.resolution: DVID provides the first steps toward distributed versioning of EM connectomics datasets, with storage tailored per data type for efficient queries, and is freely available with a growing set of storage options.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame DVID as first steps rather than a finished analog of GitHub for volumes; broader community adoption and richer moderated merge workflows remain the implied next stage.

summaries.beginner: When many people edit a giant brain map, they need a way to save versions and merge good changes, like sharing code. This paper describes free software that stores those maps so teams can branch, edit, and put improvements back together.
summaries.intermediate: Katz and Plaza present DVID in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2019) as a web-based connectomics API and distributed versioning service for EM datasets. Deployed as FlyEM’s central resource, it supports branched reconstructions for proofreader training and segmentation experiments, and backends ranging from high-speed local SSDs to cloud object stores, including laptop and large-server deployments. Tailoring storage to each connectomics data type is reported to yield efficient storage and fast queries.
summaries.advanced: The abstract claims versioning and storage flexibility but does not quantify merge conflict rates, query latency, or scale limits. DVID is positioned as first steps toward Git-like workflows, not a full moderated-acceptance social platform. Organism and dataset are unspecified here; the motivating deployment is Janelia FlyEM rather than a particular public volume named in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When many people edit a giant brain map, they need a way to save versions and merge good changes, like sharing code. This paper describes free software that stores those maps so teams can branch, edit, and put improvements back together.

ocar.opportunity: A complete Drosophila connectome requires imaging the brain, connectives, and ventral nerve cord as one contiguous specimen with contrast good enough for automated membrane segmentation and synapse detection. Until those sample-preparation problems are solved, imaging and analysis cannot even begin at whole-nervous-system scale.
ocar.challenge: The dissected CNS is too large for earlier flash-freezing methods. Three linked problems remain: keeping brain and VNC together, staining a large specimen so membranes segment automatically, and getting synapse contrast at imaging speeds that can cover the whole connectome. Conventional FIB-SEM was also slow and serial-section EM carries cutting artifacts.
ocar.action: Lu, Xu, Hayworth, Pang, Shinomiya, Plaza, Scheffer, Rubin, Hess, Rivlin, and Meinertzhagen report on bioRxiv (2019) three methods: a custom jig for microdissecting dorsal and ventral CNS with connectives; fixation and Durcupan embedment with hot-knife slicing to FIB-suitable dimensions; and heavy-metal contrast plus progressive-lowering-of-temperature dehydration. Together these target an en bloc FIB-SEM fly-brain connectome.
ocar.resolution: The procedures recover round neuronal profiles with darkly stained synapses suitable for machine segmentation and automatic synapse detection with only minimal human intervention, typically at 8 nm per voxel, and enabled a Drosophila brain FIB-SEM stack eight times faster than previously, at about serial-section rates but without cutting or section imperfections.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents these methods as enabling a whole-brain FIB-SEM connectome; applying them to the full contiguous CNS (brain plus VNC) at production throughput is the stated destination.

summaries.beginner: To map every connection in a fruit fly, the whole tiny brain must be stained so a computer can see cell outlines and contact points. This work describes new ways to dissect, stain, and image that tissue without slicing it into thousands of fragile pieces.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Lu and colleagues describe en bloc preparation of Drosophila CNS for high-throughput FIB-SEM. A custom jig keeps brain, connectives, and ventral nerve cord contiguous; hot-knife partitioning after Durcupan embedment reduces the sample to FIB-compatible chunks; heavy-metal staining and progressive-lowering-of-temperature dehydration improve contrast. They report round profiles and dark synapses suitable for automated segmentation and synapse detection, 8 nm voxels, and an eight-fold speedup versus prior FIB-SEM, comparable to serial-section rates without sectioning artifacts.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint; the eight-fold speedup and “minimal human intervention” claims are not accompanied here by error rates or a completed whole-CNS connectome. Hot-knife partitioning trades a contiguous dissection for later volume stitching. The abstract’s usual resolution of 8 nm per voxel should not be read as isotropic proof without the full methods. Dataset tagging to VNC resources is consistent with the contiguous CNS goal but the reported stack is described as Drosophila brain.

plain_language_summary: To map every connection in a fruit fly, the whole tiny brain must be stained so a computer can see cell outlines and contact points. This work describes new ways to dissect, stain, and image that tissue without slicing it into thousands of fragile pieces.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron segmentation from electron microscopy is the bottleneck between imaging a volume and assembling a connectome. A method that is both more accurate and scalable enough for very large EM volumes would let reconstruction keep pace with data collection.
ocar.challenge: Affinity prediction plus agglomeration must remain topologically correct, but earlier structured losses were computationally heavy (quadratic) and could inject spurious gradients early in training. The same method also needs to work on both nearly isotropic block-face EM and anisotropic serial-section EM.
ocar.action: Funke, Tschopp, Grisaitis, Sheridan, Singh, Saalfeld, and Turaga present in IEEE TPAMI (2019) a 3D U-Net that predicts voxel affinities, trained with a Malis-based structured loss, followed by iterative region agglomeration. They introduce a quasi-linear loss gradient and a two-pass gradient to avoid early spurious contributions, then use simple learning-free percentile-based agglomeration.
ocar.resolution: On three diverse EM datasets they report relative improvements of 27, 15, and 250 percent over previous results. Predictions are accurate enough that simple agglomeration outperforms more involved methods used on inferior predictions. Runtime scales linearly and they report about 2.6 seconds per megavoxel.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest a single method can serve both isotropic block-face and anisotropic serial-section EM, qualifying it for very large datasets; independent tests on additional volumes would stress that claim.

summaries.beginner: Computers must color in every neuron in a 3D brain picture without breaking or gluing cells wrongly. This paper trains a network to judge which tiny cubes of the picture belong together, then groups them, and reports large accuracy gains on three test sets.
summaries.intermediate: Funke et al. in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (2019) combine 3D U-Net affinity prediction with structured Malis loss and iterative agglomeration. A quasi-linear gradient and two-pass scheme address cost and early-training artifacts; percentile-based agglomeration then suffices. They report 27%, 15%, and 250% relative improvements on three EM datasets, linear scaling, and ~2.6 s/megavoxel throughput, arguing the approach fits both block-face and serial-section EM.
summaries.advanced: Relative improvements of 27, 15, and 250 percent are dataset-specific and not named in the abstract; the 250% figure especially should not be generalized. “Learning-free” agglomeration success depends on the improved affinities. The abstract does not report merge/split path-length metrics used in later connectomics bakeoffs. Organism is unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Computers must color in every neuron in a 3D brain picture without breaking or gluing cells wrongly. This paper trains a network to judge which tiny cubes of the picture belong together, then groups them, and reports large accuracy gains on three test sets.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput EM can now reconstruct mammalian circuits at synaptic resolution, but wiring diagrams lack physiological weights: it has been unknown how synapse structure maps onto transmission strength, limiting inference of function from connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Assigning a strength to each reconstructed synapse requires pairing physiology of identified connections with complete ultrastructure of every putative contact between the same cells. Quantal properties of neocortical synapses were also contested, including whether release is univesicular.
ocar.action: Holler, Köstinger, Martin, Schuhknecht, and Stratford combine, in Nature (row year 2019), slice electrophysiology of synaptically connected pyramidal neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex with correlated light microscopy and high-resolution EM of all putative synaptic contacts between the recorded neurons.
ocar.resolution: They find a linear relationship between synapse size and strength, providing a missing link for weighting EM-reconstructed synapses. Quantal analysis indicates synapses contain at least 2.7 neurotransmitter-release sites on average, supporting multivesicular release and greater computational capacity of neocortical synapses than often assumed.
ocar.future_work: The size–strength rule, if it generalizes beyond this cortical connection class, would let future EM connectomes carry physiological weights; testing other synapse types and in vivo conditions is the natural sequel implied by the result.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram lists contacts but not how strong each one is. These authors recorded from connected mouse brain cells and then photographed those same contacts in the electron microscope, finding that bigger contacts are stronger.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2019 in this catalog), Holler et al. paired slice physiology of connected mouse somatosensory pyramidal neurons with correlated light and electron microscopy of all putative contacts. They report a linear size–strength relationship and, via quantal analysis, at least 2.7 release sites per synapse on average, challenging univesicular models and supporting multivesicular release. The abstract frames this as expanding the computational power of canonical cortical microcircuitry.
summaries.advanced: The linear relation is demonstrated for this recorded pyramidal–pyramidal class in mouse somatosensory cortex, not for all synapse types. The bound “at least 2.7 release sites on average” is a quantal-analysis result and depends on that model’s assumptions. Catalog tags pointing at C. elegans do not match the abstract, which is unambiguously mouse cortex; this annotation follows the abstract. In vivo weights and other layers or species are not shown here.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram lists contacts but not how strong each one is. These authors recorded from connected mouse brain cells and then photographed those same contacts in the electron microscope, finding that bigger contacts are stronger.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics from volume EM needs not only synapse locations but also which two partners communicate at each cleft. Solving partner identity would complete the wiring graph after cleft detection.
ocar.challenge: Prior systems located synapses and only recently tried to name partners. The task is hard because the correct pre- and postsynaptic processes must be recovered from local image context around a cleft, including in dense mouse cortical neuropil.
ocar.action: Turner, Lee, Lu, Wu, Ih, and Seung reframe partner identification as generating partner masks from a given cleft. They train a convolutional net that takes local image context plus a binary cleft mask (as an attentional gate) and outputs two binary masks labeling pre- and postsynaptic partner voxels. They evaluate on mouse somatosensory cortex as part of a combined cleft-and-connection system.
ocar.resolution: An implementation of this attentional voxel-association approach is reported to perform well on a mouse somatosensory cortex dataset when used together with cleft prediction.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not quantify remaining error; integrating the partner net into fully automated, large-volume pipelines is the implied next use.

summaries.beginner: Finding a contact between two brain cells is not enough: you must know which cell is talking and which is listening. This paper trains a computer to paint those two cells from a picture of the contact itself.
summaries.intermediate: Turner et al. at the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (2019) train a convolutional network for synaptic partner assignment. Input is local volume-EM context plus a cleft mask that gates attention; outputs are pre- and postsynaptic voxel masks. They report that the method performs well on mouse somatosensory cortex as part of a combined cleft-and-connection predictor.
summaries.advanced: “Performs well” is not accompanied by precision/recall numbers in the abstract. Success is evaluated on one mouse somatosensory dataset and depends on a provided or predicted cleft mask. The method assigns partners locally and does not by itself guarantee neuron-wide identity after segmentation errors.

plain_language_summary: Finding a contact between two brain cells is not enough: you must know which cell is talking and which is listening. This paper trains a computer to paint those two cells from a picture of the contact itself.

ocar.opportunity: Micro-connectomics now reconstructs 3D neuronal networks from EM image stacks with help from deep convolutional nets, and several labs have built CNN segmentation pipelines. Those pipelines are typically too complex for non-programmers, limiting who can use automated segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Ground-truth generation, training, inference, postprocessing, proofreading, and visualization are scattered across tools and usually require Python and CNN-framework expertise. Wrapping both 2D architectures and a representative 3D neuron segmentation method in one environment is a software-engineering as much as an algorithms problem.
ocar.action: Urakubo, Bullmann, Kubota, Oba, and Ishii introduce UNI-EM in Scientific Reports (2019): a software collection covering the CNN segmentation workflow. It incorporates 2D U-Net, ResNet, HighwayNet, and DenseNet, and wraps flood-filling networks as a 3D neuron segmentation algorithm, with example workflows for mitochondria (2D CNN) and neurons (FFNs).
ocar.resolution: UNI-EM is presented as enabling CNN-based EM segmentation, including state-of-the-art-level 2D and 3D methods, without requiring knowledge of Python or CNN frameworks, via the example workflows.
ocar.future_work: The authors position UNI-EM as an environment rather than a new accuracy record; sustaining wrappers as FFN and 2D architectures evolve is the practical sequel.

summaries.beginner: Cutting-edge computer tools for tracing cells in electron-microscope pictures are usually only usable by programmers. This paper packages those tools so biologists can train and run them by following example recipes, without writing code.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2019), Urakubo et al. present UNI-EM, integrating ground-truth generation, training, inference, postprocessing, proofreading, and visualization. Supported 2D nets include U-Net, ResNet, HighwayNet, and DenseNet; flood-filling networks are wrapped for 3D neuron segmentation. Example workflows cover mitochondria segmentation with a 2D CNN and neuron segmentation with FFNs, aimed at users without Python or CNN-framework knowledge.
summaries.advanced: “State-of-the-art level” refers to the wrapped published architectures, not a new leaderboard result in this paper. Accessibility claims are not accompanied by user studies in the abstract. FFN wrapping implies the known computational cost of that method. Organism and dataset are unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Cutting-edge computer tools for tracing cells in electron-microscope pictures are usually only usable by programmers. This paper packages those tools so biologists can train and run them by following example recipes, without writing code.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is a core neuroscience model, but quantitative connectivity covering all connections from sensory input to end-organ output in both adult sexes—the information needed to model behavior—had not been fully available. Sex differences in structure and connectivity were also incompletely mapped, including the male head.
ocar.challenge: Prior reconstructions left gaps, especially for the male, and did not provide whole-animal matrices spanning both sexes. Neurons that are shared between sexes may still differ in structure, edge strength, or how sex-specific circuitry joins central pathways.
ocar.action: Cook, Jarrell, Brittin, Wang, Bloniarz, Yakovlev, Nguyen, Tang, Bayer, Duerr, Bülow, Hobert, Hall, and Emmons present in Nature (2019) serial-EM reconstructions using new and previously published electron micrographs, updating earlier results and adding male-head data, to produce quantitative connectivity matrices for both adult sexes.
ocar.resolution: They report whole-animal connectomes encompassing all connections from sensory input to end-organ output. The nervous system differs between sexes at multiple levels: some sex-shared neurons in sexual-behavior circuits are dimorphic in structure and connectivity; sex-specific inputs converge on central circuitry; and a substantial number of connections in sex-shared central pathways differ in strength.
ocar.future_work: These quantitative matrices are offered as a basis for modeling how complex, adaptive behavior is generated; comparing individuals and linking edges to function are the implied next uses.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans has a simple enough nervous system that every connection can be listed. This paper maps that wiring in both adult sexes and shows that males and hermaphrodites are not wired identically, even for cells they share.
summaries.intermediate: Cook et al. in Nature (2019) report whole-animal C. elegans connectomes for both adult sexes from serial electron microscopy, combining new and published micrographs and including male-head data. Matrices span sensory input to end-organ output. Findings include structural and connectivity dimorphism in some sex-shared neurons, convergence of sex-specific onto central circuitry, and many strength differences in sex-shared central pathways.
summaries.advanced: “All connections” is the authors’ claim for these reconstructions; historical C. elegans connectomes have had residual gaps, and this abstract does not quantify remaining uncertainty. Strength differences are reported as substantial in number, not with effect sizes here. Behavior is a motivation, not a result of this paper. The work updates White-style serial EM rather than replacing it with a new imaging modality.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans has a simple enough nervous system that every connection can be listed. This paper maps that wiring in both adult sexes and shows that males and hermaphrodites are not wired identically, even for cells they share.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can now remap C. elegans connectomes with higher throughput and less subjectivity than White and colleagues’ fully manual reconstruction. New maps are needed to fill remaining gaps and to ask how connectivity changes with development, individuality, sexual dimorphism, and genetic or environmental factors.
ocar.challenge: A complete wiring diagram requires vEM of the entire nervous system plus associated non-neuronal tissues. Throughput, consistency, and reduced manual subjectivity are still limiting, and the pipeline must extend beyond a single canonical hermaphrodite adult.
ocar.action: Mulcahy, Witvliet, Holmyard, Mitchell, Chisholm, Meirovitch, Samuel, and Zhen describe in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) their current volume-EM pipeline for the C. elegans nervous system, with projected improvements, aimed at both gap-filling and comparative connectomes.
ocar.resolution: The paper presents a practical vEM pipeline and a roadmap for using it to study development, individuality, sexual dimorphism, and regulation of connectivity in C. elegans and beyond.
ocar.future_work: Projected pipeline improvements and application to questions of development and individuality are explicitly flagged as next steps.

summaries.beginner: The first complete worm wiring diagram was traced by hand. This article explains a modern electron-microscopy workflow meant to make new worm maps faster and more consistent, so scientists can compare animals as they grow or differ.
summaries.intermediate: Mulcahy et al. in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) outline a volume electron microscopy pipeline for the C. elegans nervous system. They contrast it with White et al. (1986) fully manual reconstruction and argue that current vEM can map new connectomes with increased throughput and reduced subjectivity. Targets include remaining gaps plus development, individuality, sexual dimorphism, and gene–environment effects.
summaries.advanced: This is a pipeline/perspective piece, not a new completed connectome. Throughput and subjectivity claims are qualitative in the abstract. “Beyond” C. elegans is aspirational. Associated non-neuronal tissues are in the definition of a complete connectome here but not quantified.

plain_language_summary: The first complete worm wiring diagram was traced by hand. This article explains a modern electron-microscopy workflow meant to make new worm maps faster and more consistent, so scientists can compare animals as they grow or differ.

ocar.opportunity: Pixel-accurate tracking of many interrelated objects in an image stack is central to connectomic instance segmentation. Existing single-object tracking, including flood-filling networks, is accurate but too computationally heavy for most laboratories at connectomic scale.
ocar.challenge: Iterated individual-object tracking or segment-then-match scales poorly when objects are numerous, complex, and mutually interlocked in EM volumes. Turning clustering into a tractable classification problem without losing pixel accuracy is the algorithmic challenge.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Mi, Saribekyan, Matveev, Rolnick, Wierzynski, and Shavit introduce cross-classification clustering (3C) at CVPR (2018): a logarithmic number of independent classifications per image whose cross-labeling uniquely assigns pixels to object labels, applied to nanoscale EM neural-tissue mapping.
ocar.resolution: They report state-of-the-art accuracy in connectomics and an order-of-magnitude scalability gain over existing single-object tracking methods such as flood-filling networks, arguing this puts high-performing reconstruction within reach of more labs. They also suggest benefits for video and medical-image segmentation.
ocar.future_work: Deployment on additional EM volumes and domains (video, medical imagery) is suggested; independent computational-cost comparisons would test the order-of-magnitude claim outside this paper.

summaries.beginner: Computers must follow many tangled cells through a stack of pictures at once. This method splits that job into a small number of simpler labeling tasks whose combination uniquely names each cell, aiming to be much cheaper than tracing one cell at a time.
summaries.intermediate: Meirovitch et al. at Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (2018) present cross-classification clustering (3C) for multi-object tracking in 3D instance segmentation. A logarithmic number of independent per-image classifications cross-label pixels onto object identities. Applied to connectomic EM, they claim state-of-the-art accuracy and roughly 10× scalability versus single-object trackers such as flood-filling networks.
summaries.advanced: “State-of-the-art accuracy” and “order of magnitude” scalability are not accompanied by named datasets or path-length error rates in the abstract. Benefits for video and medical imagery are speculative here. Comparison is specifically to single-object tracking (FFN-like), not to all contemporary agglomeration pipelines.

plain_language_summary: Computers must follow many tangled cells through a stack of pictures at once. This method splits that job into a small number of simpler labeling tasks whose combination uniquely names each cell, aiming to be much cheaper than tracing one cell at a time.

ocar.opportunity: The dense circuit structure of mammalian cerebral cortex was unknown because packing of thin processes made reconstruction of sizable neuropil out of reach. Faster 3D EM exists, but dense analysis—not imaging—has been the limit, with prior dense cortical reconstructions confined to femtoliter-scale volumes.
ocar.challenge: Automated segmentations remain too error-prone to use raw. Progress therefore depends on human–machine efficiency: better automation, directing people only to likely errors, and minimizing annotator latency. Inhibitory axon types, geometric predictability of wiring, thalamocortical innervation, and possible Hebbian imprints were all previously inaccessible at dense scale in cortex.
ocar.action: Motta, Berning, Boergens, Staffler, Beining, Loomba, Schramm, Hennig, Wissler, and Helmstaedter reconstruct in Science (2018) about 500,000 cubic micrometers of layer 4 mouse barrel cortex. They improved automated segmentation, targeted likely errors, and optimized in-browser annotation so nearly 100 student annotators solved problems in about 29 s each, investing about 4000 human hours.
ocar.resolution: They report 2.7 m of densely reconstructed neuronal wire, ~300 times larger than previous dense cortical reconstructions at ~20-fold efficiency, and a connectome among 6979 pre- and 3719 postsynaptic neurites with at least 10 synapses each (153,171 synapses in that filtered graph; ~400,000 synapses among 34,221 axons and 11,400 postsynaptic processes in the broader volume). Connectomic data defined inhibitory axon types with subcellular specificity; beyond ~5 μm geometric predictability was low and random-wiring models were rejected, while a thalamocortical synapse-density gradient increased input variability onto L4 dendrites. They also give upper bounds on the fraction of circuit consistent with saturated long-term potentiation.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose connectomic phenotyping across cortices, layers, species, developmental stages, sensory experience, and disease—screening local dense mammalian circuitry with the same approach.

summaries.beginner: A piece of mouse cortex was mapped so densely that thousands of nerve-cell branches and hundreds of thousands of contacts could be listed. The map is hundreds of times larger than earlier complete cortical reconstructions and shows that wiring is not a simple function of which branches pass near each other.
summaries.intermediate: Motta et al. in Science (2018) densely reconstruct ~500,000 μm³ of mouse L4 barrel cortex—about 300× previous dense cortical volumes—with ~4000 annotator hours and ~20× efficiency, reconstructing 2.7 m of cable. A filtered connectome (neurites with ≥10 synapses) comprises 153,171 synapses among 6979 pre- and 3719 postsynaptic neurites. They extract inhibitory/excitatory subtypes not predictable from geometry, reject coarse random wiring for dense neuropil beyond ~5 μm, describe a thalamocortical density gradient, and bound the circuit fraction consistent with saturated LTP.
summaries.advanced: Size and synapse counts mix several nested graphs (filtered ≥10-synapse neurites vs. the larger ~400,000-synapse set); they should not be conflated. “Learnedness” is an upper bound on a Hebbian-consistent fraction, not a direct LTP measurement. Geometric unpredictability beyond ~5 μm does not imply no structure at other scales. Reconstruction remains human–machine, not fully automatic. The 29 s/problem figure includes preparation and transition time as stated.

plain_language_summary: A piece of mouse cortex was mapped so densely that thousands of nerve-cell branches and hundreds of thousands of contacts could be listed. The map is hundreds of times larger than earlier complete cortical reconstructions and shows that wiring is not a simple function of which branches pass near each other.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM methods such as serial-section array tomography, serial block-face imaging, and FIB-SEM have opened 3D ultrastructure, but most remain limited to relatively small tissue volumes because standard scanning EM throughput is too low. Mapping cubic-millimeter-scale volumes at high resolution needs a different imaging architecture.
ocar.challenge: Single-beam SEM acquisition time explodes with area. Even with automated preparation robots, imaging large sample areas at connectomic resolution has been the bottleneck for cubic-millimeter mapping, including ambitions associated with large mouse volumes.
ocar.action: Eberle and Zeidler review in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018) volume-EM approaches with emphasis on serial-section array tomography and newly commercialized multi-beam scanning electron microscopes optimized for large-area imaging, complemented by automated sample-preparation robots.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that multi-beam SEM plus automated preparation puts mapping of larger, cubic-millimeter-range tissue volumes at high resolution within reach, providing a mini-review of the volume-imaging landscape.
ocar.future_work: The review frames cubic-millimeter mapping as newly realistic rather than completed; actual end-to-end connectomes on that scale still depend on sectioning, alignment, and analysis beyond the microscope.

summaries.beginner: Photographing a large piece of brain at the detail of individual connections takes far too long with a usual electron microscope. This short review describes cameras that use many beams at once so much bigger samples can be imaged.
summaries.intermediate: Eberle and Zeidler in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018) review 3D EM methods—array tomography, serial block-face imaging, and FIB-SEM—and focus on multi-beam scanning EM for large-area imaging. Combined with automated preparation robots, they argue cubic-millimeter-scale high-resolution mapping is now within reach. The piece is a mini-review rather than a new instrument paper.
summaries.advanced: “Within reach” is prospective. Throughput numbers are not given in the abstract. Multi-beam SEM addresses acquisition area, not proofreading. Catalog association with MICrONS/mouse reflects the cubic-millimeter motivation but this paper is not a MICrONS dataset release.

plain_language_summary: Photographing a large piece of brain at the detail of individual connections takes far too long with a usual electron microscope. This short review describes cameras that use many beams at once so much bigger samples can be imaged.

ocar.opportunity: Recent EM imaging and segmentation quality mean many segments are largely correct, yet remaining errors must be proofread in multi-terabyte volumes where some objects span several gigavoxels and several people must work at once. Tools built for tracing small, dirty segmentations do not match this regime.
ocar.challenge: Proofreaders need low-latency 3D views of huge mutable objects, ways to split very large false merges, collaboration with concurrency control, and history tracking—without chopping the dataset into isolated subsets. Scaling the client against a high-performance image database is required.
ocar.action: Zhao, Olbris, Yu, and Plaza introduce NeuTu in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) as a DVID client for collaborative, segmentation-based proofreading. Distinguishing features include low-latency 3D visualization of large mutable segmentations, interactive splitting of large false merges, 3D bookmarks, proofreading-history visualization, and lock-based real-time collaboration.
ocar.resolution: These features allowed managing proofreading of a large dataset without dividing it into subsets, and NeuTu is credited with enabling some of the largest fly-brain connectome reconstructions as well as discoveries in the fly brain.
ocar.future_work: The software is presented as a working production client; further scaling with dataset size and concurrent users is implicit in the DVID-backed design.

summaries.beginner: After a computer paints neurons in a giant fly-brain picture, people still have to fix mistakes, including huge wrongly glued cells, while working together. This paper describes a program built for that team-editing job.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao et al. in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) present NeuTu, a DVID client for collaborative proofreading of large, high-quality EM segmentations. It targets multi-TB volumes with largely correct but gigavoxel-scale segments and simultaneous users. Features include fast 3D visualization, semi-automatic split of large false merges, 3D investigation marks, history views, and lock-based concurrency. The authors report it enabled some of the largest fly connectome reconstructions without subsetting the volume.
summaries.advanced: Impact claims (“largest reconstructions,” “interesting discoveries”) are not quantified here. Lock-based concurrency can serialize work on contested objects. NeuTu assumes a DVID backend. Organism is fly in the resolution statement, not a named public dataset in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: After a computer paints neurons in a giant fly-brain picture, people still have to fix mistakes, including huge wrongly glued cells, while working together. This paper describes a program built for that team-editing job.

ocar.opportunity: Dense synaptic reconstruction in model brains is becoming feasible, as genomics once was, because of FIB-SEM, better alignment, and computer-aided neuron reconstruction. Drosophila is a leading case: cell numbers are manageable and neuron classes are genetically identifiable, so a complete adult and larval connectome can change how behavior is explained.
ocar.challenge: Human proofreading of segmented bodies remains the most time-consuming step. Distinguishing major pathways (≥100 presynaptic contacts) from minor ones (fewer than about 10), and the fact that most neurites are both pre- and postsynaptic with multiple postsynaptic partners at each site, complicates interpretation.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2018), offers a personal perspective on Drosophila connectomics: progress in EM circuits across fly brain regions, the near-term prospect of complete adult and larval connectomes, and how silencing or activating identified neurons can link circuits to behavior—and reveal unsuspected pathways that predict new behaviors.
ocar.resolution: He argues that complete fly connectomes will support causal tests of behavior, comparative evolutionary circuits, and eventually vertebrate strategies, including disorders with a connectomic basis. Recent advances are described as destined to reveal the complete adult connectome within a few years, possibly sooner in the larva.
ocar.future_work: The remaining bottleneck highlighted is human proofreading; applying circuit maps to individual differences and to vertebrate brains is explicitly prospective.

summaries.beginner: A complete list of connections in a fruit-fly brain is becoming realistic. This essay asks what that list is good for: turning identified circuits on and off to explain behavior, and spotting pathways no one knew to look for.
summaries.intermediate: Meinertzhagen’s Journal of Experimental Biology (2018) perspective reviews Drosophila dense-circuit EM, especially FIB-SEM, alignment, and reconstruction. He distinguishes major (≥100 contacts) versus minor (fewer than about 10) pathways, notes mixed pre/post neurites and polyadic synapses, and flags human proofreading as rate-limiting. He predicts complete adult and larval connectomes on a few-year timescale and stresses causal behavior tests via genetic access plus discovery of unanticipated pathways.
summaries.advanced: This is opinion/perspective, not new data. Timeline predictions are historical from 2018. Numeric thresholds (100 vs ~10) are heuristic. Catalog tags include Drosophila larva and FIB-SEM; the essay spans larva and adult. Causal “loss or gain” of behavior still requires physiology and behavior, which the connectome alone does not provide—as the author notes.

plain_language_summary: A complete list of connections in a fruit-fly brain is becoming realistic. This essay asks what that list is good for: turning identified circuits on and off to explain behavior, and spotting pathways no one knew to look for.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic annotation of synapses has succeeded in near-isotropic vertebrate EM, but results on non-isotropic insect volume EM were not yet on par with human annotation. Mapping synaptic clefts across a complete Drosophila brain would remove a major manual bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Serial transmission or scanning EM of insect brains is anisotropic, so isotropic-field-of-view 3D networks can be a poor fit. Training data are local (CREMI challenge clefts) while the target volume is huge (50 tera-voxels) and far from the training region.
ocar.action: Heinrich, Funke, Pape, Nunez-Iglesias, and Saalfeld design a 3D U-Net for isotropic fields of view in non-isotropic data, train by regression on a signed distance transform of manual CREMI synaptic clefts, and build open-source software for optimized parallel prediction on very large volumes, applying it to a 50 tera-voxel complete Drosophila brain.
ocar.resolution: They observe significant improvement over the state of the art on the challenge setting and report that the model generalizes well to areas far from available training data on the whole-brain volume.
ocar.future_work: Whole-brain cleft maps still need integration with partner assignment and proofreading; the abstract emphasizes generalization away from training regions as the enabling result.

summaries.beginner: Computers are good at finding connections in some 3D brain pictures but weaker when the slices are much coarser in one direction, as in many insect datasets. This work retrains a 3D network for that situation and runs it on a complete fruit-fly brain image.
summaries.intermediate: Heinrich et al. at MICCAI (2018) introduce a 3D U-Net tailored to anisotropic volume EM, trained by signed-distance regression on CREMI synaptic-cleft annotations. Parallel prediction software is applied to a 50 tera-voxel complete Drosophila brain. They report significant gains over prior automatic cleft methods and good generalization far from the training territory.
summaries.advanced: “Significant improvement” is not given as a numeric score in the abstract. Generalization “well” is qualitative. CREMI is Drosophila but not the whole brain; domain shift remains a caveat even with the claimed transfer. Cleft detection is not full synapse-to-partner connectome reconstruction. Fly organism tag matches; no named registry dataset in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Computers are good at finding connections in some 3D brain pictures but weaker when the slices are much coarser in one direction, as in many insect datasets. This work retrains a 3D network for that situation and runs it on a complete fruit-fly brain image.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM now generates very large image datasets efficiently, but analysis software has not kept up. Annotating and editing segmentations in volumes approaching the petabyte range needs a tool that remains interactive.
ocar.challenge: Most viewers choke on large voxel data. Users still need both fully manual and semi-automatic labeling, plus real-time exploration, without a heavyweight pipeline.
ocar.action: Berger, Seung, and Lichtman introduce VAST (Volume Annotation and Segmentation Tool) in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018): a freely available utility for generating and editing annotations and segmentations of large volumetric image datasets, with a simple interface aimed at real-time exploration even in the petabyte range.
ocar.resolution: VAST is presented as an efficient manual and semi-automatic labeling tool for large 3D stacks, freely available.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not detail collaboration or automated proofreading; those remain outside this utility’s stated scope.

summaries.beginner: Huge stacks of brain pictures are hard even to open, let alone to color in by hand. This paper offers a free program designed so people can still browse and label those stacks smoothly, including extremely large ones.
summaries.intermediate: Berger, Seung, and Lichtman in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) present VAST, a free tool for manual and semi-automatic annotation and segmentation of large voxel datasets from serial-section EM. They emphasize a simple interface and real-time exploration even for data in the petabyte range. The program is aimed at analysis that has lagged behind efficient generation of very large EM stacks.
summaries.advanced: Petabyte-range interactivity is claimed without hardware benchmarks in the abstract. VAST is a labeling utility, not a distributed proofreading platform. Organism and dataset are unspecified. Semi-automatic methods are named but not specified here.

plain_language_summary: Huge stacks of brain pictures are hard even to open, let alone to color in by hand. This paper offers a free program designed so people can still browse and label those stacks smoothly, including extremely large ones.

ocar.opportunity: Leech ganglia are homologous from animal to animal, so an EM connectome of one ganglion could be checked against physiology in another—confirming known synapses, challenging others, and discovering new ones that can then be recorded. Combining connectomics with electrophysiology would show how circuits produce behavior in this classical system.
ocar.challenge: Direct physiology cannot easily map large numbers of connections, yet anatomy alone cannot verify function. Some physiologically described connections might be absent anatomically, and uncharacterized neurons need a path from EM partners to recordings in adult ganglia.
ocar.action: Pipkin, Bushong, Ellisman, and Kristan collect a serial block-face EM volume of an entire juvenile leech ganglion, reconstruct a well-characterized swim motor-neuron circuit to locate synapses, then reconstruct an uncharacterized neuron and a presynaptic partner and test that pair with intracellular recordings in an adult ganglion.
ocar.resolution: They confirm multiple, widely distributed synaptic contacts between connected pairs and verify anatomical counterparts of known longitudinal muscle motor-neuron connections, while some physiological connections were not present anatomically. The EM-discovered pair was also functional physiologically, demonstrating complementary value of anatomy and physiology.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as groundwork for future behavioral studies using the same combined approach.

summaries.beginner: A leech’s repeating nerve clusters are similar from animal to animal. Researchers mapped one cluster with an electron microscope, checked known connections, found a new one, and then recorded from the same cell types in another animal to show the new contact really works.
summaries.intermediate: Pipkin et al. (bioRxiv 2018; catalog journal field) use SBEM of a juvenile leech ganglion to reconstruct swim-related motor neurons and their synapses. They confirm multiple distributed contacts among connected pairs and anatomical presence of some, but not all, previously physiological connections. An uncharacterized neuron plus an EM-identified presynaptic partner yielded a functional synapse when recorded in an adult ganglion, arguing for combined connectomics and electrophysiology.
summaries.advanced: Absence of an anatomical synapse for some physiological connections could reflect reconstruction limits, developmental stage (juvenile EM vs adult physiology), or true mismatch—the abstract does not decide. Homology across animals is assumed. Catalog lists Frontiers-style DOI with bioRxiv as journal in this shard; treat as preprint/report of the SBEM-plus-physiology study. Organism is leech, not a registry dataset here.

plain_language_summary: A leech’s repeating nerve clusters are similar from animal to animal. Researchers mapped one cluster with an electron microscope, checked known connections, found a new one, and then recorded from the same cell types in another animal to show the new contact really works.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s roughly 100,000-neuron brain is large but tractable for comprehensive circuit mapping, and only EM can map synaptic connectivity completely and without prior bias. A whole adult brain EM volume would accelerate fly neuroscience if it can be imaged at all—the brain is too large for conventional EM.
ocar.challenge: Conventional EM cannot cover an adult fly brain. After imaging, brain-spanning circuits still need validation; olfactory inputs to the mushroom body were incomplete, including unidentified drivers of Kenyon cells and poorly resolved axonal clustering relative to light microscopy.
ocar.action: Zheng, Lauritzen, Perlman, Robinson, Nichols, Milkie, Torrens, Price, Fisher, Sharifi, Calle-Schuler, Kmecova, Ali, Karsh, Trautman, Bogovic, Hanslovsky, Jefferis, Kazhdan, Khairy, Saalfeld, Fetter, and Bock developed a custom high-throughput EM platform and imaged the entire brain of an adult female fly, then traced mushroom-body-related circuitry. They also built a pipeline to search EM-traced skeletons against large light-microscopy morphology databases.
ocar.resolution: They describe the complete set of olfactory inputs to the MB, a new cell type (MB-CP2) providing microglomerular driving input to Kenyon cells, neurons postsynaptic to Kenyon-cell dendrites, tighter axonal clustering in the calyx than light-level data indicated, and that primary postsynaptic targets of KCs in the MB are other KCs and the APL neuron. The dataset is freely available.
ocar.future_work: The volume is offered to accelerate further circuit mapping; matching EM skeletons to genetic driver lines via the LM search pipeline is an explicit next use.

summaries.beginner: Researchers photographed an entire adult fruit-fly brain with an electron microscope for the first time at this scale. They checked the data by tracing smell-and-learning circuits and released the images so others can map more pathways.
summaries.intermediate: Zheng et al. (Cell DOI; catalog venue bioRxiv 2017) report a complete adult female Drosophila brain EM volume from a custom high-throughput platform. Validation traces olfactory inputs to the mushroom body, identifies MB-CP2 as a multimodal microglomerular input to Kenyon cells, finds KC-to-KC and KC-to-APL as primary postsynaptic targets in the MB, and reports tighter projection-neuron clustering in the calyx than light microscopy suggested. A software pipeline matches EM skeletons to LM databases for cell-type and driver-line identification. Data are freely available.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” refers to imaging coverage of one adult female brain, not a fully proofread connectome in this paper. Circuit results are MB-focused validation, not whole-brain reconstruction. Clustering versus light microscopy depends on registration quality. Catalog year/venue may reflect preprint vs Cell publication; pedagogical text follows the abstract’s claims without adding later FlyWire numbers.

plain_language_summary: Researchers photographed an entire adult fruit-fly brain with an electron microscope for the first time at this scale. They checked the data by tracing smell-and-learning circuits and released the images so others can map more pathways.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila mushroom body is the major site of associative learning, but understanding memory formation, storage, and retrieval requires a synaptic-resolution wiring diagram of identified neurons in its compartments. The α lobe’s three functional units were a natural, complete target.
ocar.challenge: Sparse Kenyon-cell coding, compartmentalized output, and dopaminergic teaching signals were known in outline, but not the full morphologies and synapses of all neurons in those compartments, including unexpected connection classes.
ocar.action: Takemura, Aso, Hige, Wong, Lu, Xu, Rivlin, Hess, Zhao, Parag, Berg, Huang, Katz, Olbris, Plaza, Umayam, Aniceto, Chang, Lauchie, Ogundeyi, Ordish, Shinomiya, Sigmund, Takemura, Tran, Turner, Rubin, and Scheffer reconstructed all 983 neurons within the three compartments of the adult MB α lobe from isotropic 8 nm FIB-SEM voxels, mapping morphologies and synaptic connections.
ocar.resolution: Each Kenyon cell makes multiple en passant synapses onto MB output neurons in each compartment; some MBONs sample all KCs, others are modality-biased. Only 6% of KC→MBON synapses receive a direct dopaminergic synapse. They identify unanticipated KC→DAN and DAN→MBON synapses; DAN activation slowly depolarizes the MBON and can weaken memory recall.
ocar.future_work: The unexpected DAN–MBON and KC–DAN connections, plus the 6% figure, set up functional tests of how reinforcement is delivered and how recall is modulated at identified synapses.

summaries.beginner: The mushroom body is the fruit fly’s main learning center. This team listed every nerve cell in one part of it and every contact among them, and found some connection types that models of learning had not featured.
summaries.intermediate: Takemura et al. in eLife (2017) reconstruct all 983 neurons in three adult Drosophila mushroom-body α-lobe compartments from 8 nm isotropic FIB-SEM. KCs make multiple en passant synapses onto MBONs; MBON sampling can be all-to-one or modality-specific. Direct DAN synapses hit only 6% of KC→MBON synapses. Newly emphasized KC→DAN and DAN→MBON synapses are reported; DAN activation yields slow MBON depolarization and can weaken memory recall.
summaries.advanced: The connectome is the α lobe’s three compartments, not the whole MB. The 6% statistic is specific to KC→MBON synapses receiving a direct DAN synapse. Physiological DAN→MBON effects are reported in the abstract but the full conditions are not. Isotropic 8 nm FIB-SEM is the imaging substrate (SEM tag in the catalog is coarser than the methods).

plain_language_summary: The mushroom body is the fruit fly’s main learning center. This team listed every nerve cell in one part of it and every contact among them, and found some connection types that models of learning had not featured.

ocar.opportunity: 3D neuron reconstruction from EM, and image segmentation more generally, still produces split and merge errors. Nets that detect those errors on a candidate object, and nets that correct them, could focus human proofreading and improve automated output.
ocar.challenge: Both tasks must use the raw image plus a binary mask of a candidate object. Error correction is framed as object-mask pruning, assuming the candidate is a superset of the true object—an assumption that fails if the candidate is missing pieces. Training 3D multiscale nets that actually raise accuracy is non-trivial.
ocar.action: Zung, Tartavull, Lee, and Seung define error-detection and error-correction tasks at NeurIPS (2017) and train multiscale 3D convolutional networks for both. Detection outputs a map of split and merge errors; correction outputs the true object. They also feed the detecting net’s “advice” (union of erroneous objects) into the correcting net.
ocar.resolution: The error-detecting net can achieve high accuracy. The error-correcting net’s accuracy is enhanced when its input mask is advice from the detector.
ocar.future_work: The pruning assumption and remaining residual errors imply that detection-guided human or automated correction still needs evaluation on full neurite reconstructions, not only object masks.

summaries.beginner: Computer tracings of brain cells still split one cell into pieces or glue two cells together. This work trains one network to point at those mistakes and another to fix them, using the original picture plus the computer’s first guess.
summaries.intermediate: Zung et al. at Neural Information Processing Systems (2017) train multiscale 3D convolutional nets for EM neuron error detection and correction. Detection predicts split/merge error maps on a candidate mask; correction performs object-mask pruning toward the true object. Detector accuracy is described as high; correction improves when the input is the union of objects the detector flags as erroneous.
summaries.advanced: “High accuracy” is not numeric in the abstract. Correction assumes the candidate is a superset of the truth (pruning), so missing fragments (splits that omit the true piece from the mask) are out of scope for that net. No organism or dataset is named. This is a framework paper, not a production proofreading system.

plain_language_summary: Computer tracings of brain cells still split one cell into pieces or glue two cells together. This work trains one network to point at those mistakes and another to fix them, using the original picture plus the computer’s first guess.

ocar.opportunity: Teravoxel volume-EM datasets of neural tissue can now be acquired in weeks, but analysis still takes years of manual labor. Automatically inferring a richly annotated synaptic connectivity matrix from skeleton reconstructions would change that bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Beyond tracing neurites, one must identify mitochondria, synapses and types, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types. Doing so consistently across species (zebrafish, mouse, zebra finch) and then computing a real circuit (songbird basal ganglia) is a combined vision and neuroscience problem.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Schubert, Killinger, Urban, Mikula, Svara, and Kornfeld present SyConn in Nature Methods (2017): deep convolutional nets and random forests that annotate those structures from manual neurite skeletons. They test on SBEM datasets from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch and compute synaptic wiring of songbird basal ganglia.
ocar.resolution: They report, for example, that basal-ganglia cell types with high in vivo firing rates had higher densities of mitochondria and vesicles, and that synapse sizes and quantities scaled systematically with innervated postsynaptic cell types.
ocar.future_work: The framework still starts from manual skeletons; fully automated skeletons plus SyConn-style annotation is the natural extension implied by the acquisition-versus-analysis mismatch.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope volumes of brain can be collected far faster than people can label every synapse and organelle. This software uses machine learning to tag those parts on already-traced cell skeletons and then list who connects to whom, demonstrated in fish, mouse, and songbird tissue.
summaries.intermediate: Dorkenwald et al. in Nature Methods (2017) introduce SyConn, using CNNs and random forests to infer an annotated synaptic connectivity matrix from manual neurite skeletons—identifying mitochondria, synapse types, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types. Tests include SBEM from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch, plus songbird basal-ganglia wiring. They link high in vivo firing-rate cell types to higher mitochondrial and vesicle densities and report systematic scaling of synapse size and number with postsynaptic cell type.
summaries.advanced: Inputs are manual skeletons, so tracing labor is reduced but not eliminated. Cross-species tests are named but accuracy metrics are not in the abstract. In vivo firing-rate correlations are example findings, not a complete physiology dataset here. Songbird basal ganglia is the featured circuit computation.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope volumes of brain can be collected far faster than people can label every synapse and organelle. This software uses machine learning to tag those parts on already-traced cell skeletons and then list who connects to whom, demonstrated in fish, mouse, and songbird tissue.

ocar.opportunity: Throughout postembryonic growth, circuits must keep producing appropriate output as the body enlarges. Whether structural adaptation of morphology and synapses conserves computation—for example, locating a nociceptive stimulus—was unclear, even in Drosophila larva where detailed morphology had been measured.
ocar.challenge: Comparing identified circuits across developmental stages requires serial-section EM volumes of the same cell types in different animals (here 1st versus 3rd instar) and a way to interpret five-fold interneuron growth without losing cell-type-specific input fractions.
ocar.action: Gerhard, Andrade, Fetter, Cardona, and Schneider-Mizell reconstruct an identified nociceptive circuit in two Drosophila larvae (1st and 3rd instar) from new and existing ssEM volumes, comparing morphology and connectivity across postembryonic development.
ocar.resolution: They find extremely consistent, topographically arranged circuit structure: five-fold interneuron growth was offset so cell-type-specific inputs remained a stable fraction of total input, while more synaptic contacts came with a disproportionate increase in small dendritic terminal branches. They propose these growth patterns conserve computational function.
ocar.future_work: The proposal that structure conserves function (e.g., nociceptive localization) invites physiological tests across instars; the study itself is comparative anatomy of two larvae.

summaries.beginner: As a young fruit-fly maggot grows, its nerve cells get bigger, yet it still needs the same kinds of reflexes. Comparing the same pain-sensing circuit in a tiny larva and a larger one, the authors find the wiring pattern stays the same in relative terms.
summaries.intermediate: Gerhard et al. on bioRxiv (2017) reconstruct an identified Drosophila larval nociceptive circuit in 1st- and 3rd-instar animals with serial-section EM. Circuit topography is highly consistent. Five-fold interneuron growth is offset so cell-type-specific inputs remain a stable fraction of total input; synapse number rises with extra small dendritic terminal branches. They propose this conserves computation such as stimulus location.
summaries.advanced: n = two larvae (one per instar). “Extremely consistent” is qualitative. Conservation of function is a proposal, not a behavioral or physiological result. The work extends Schneider-Mizell et al. 2016 morphology measurements. Dataset tag DS03 Drosophila larva matches.

plain_language_summary: As a young fruit-fly maggot grows, its nerve cells get bigger, yet it still needs the same kinds of reflexes. Comparing the same pain-sensing circuit in a tiny larva and a larger one, the authors find the wiring pattern stays the same in relative terms.

ocar.opportunity: Sequential neural activation is seen in many brain areas, but the underlying network structure is rarely known. Zebra finch HVC generates sequences that pace song, so mapping which cell types HVC(RA) axons contact near versus far from the soma could distinguish models of sequence generation.
ocar.challenge: Electrical paired recordings had suggested near-soma connectivity onto inhibitory cells, but long-range excitatory targets were inaccessible that way. Combining serial block-face EM with light microscopy is needed to score target cell types as a function of distance along the axon.
ocar.action: Kornfeld, Benezra, Narayanan, Svara, Egger, Oberlaender, Denk, and Long combine SBEM with light microscopy in eLife (2017) to identify cell types targeted by HVC(RA) neurons that control song timing in zebra finch.
ocar.resolution: Close to the soma, axons almost exclusively targeted inhibitory interneurons, matching paired recordings. Far from the soma, targets were mostly other excitatory neurons, about half of them other HVC(RA) cells. Both observations fit global synaptic chains in HVC embedded in local inhibitory networks as a way to pace song.
ocar.future_work: The anatomical pattern supports chain-like sequence models but does not itself record sequences; linking these synapses to in vivo sequence activity is the implied next step.

summaries.beginner: Birdsong is paced by a brain area whose cells fire in order, but the wiring that makes that order was unclear. Electron-microscope maps show nearby contacts mostly go to braking cells, while farther contacts mostly go to other pacing cells.
summaries.intermediate: Kornfeld et al. in eLife (2017) use serial block-face EM plus light microscopy to map HVC(RA) axonal targets in zebra finch. Proximal axons almost exclusively hit inhibitory interneurons, consistent with paired physiology; distal targets are mostly excitatory, about half other HVC(RA) cells. They interpret this as global excitatory synaptic chains embedded in local inhibitory networks for song timing.
summaries.advanced: “Almost exclusively” and “about half” are the abstract’s quantitative hedges; sample sizes are not given here. Function (sequence generation) is inferential from anatomy plus prior physiology. Organism is songbird (catalog: other / DS19 songbird). Preparation/sectioning tags match SBEM.

plain_language_summary: Birdsong is paced by a brain area whose cells fire in order, but the wiring that makes that order was unclear. Electron-microscope maps show nearby contacts mostly go to braking cells, while farther contacts mostly go to other pacing cells.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM yields 3D images with superior z-resolution and little need for registration, which would help trace small processes and reduce proofreading in connectomics. Wider adoption has been blocked by slow imaging and poor long-term stability, which cap acquisition volume.
ocar.challenge: Months-long operation and continuously imaged volumes above 10^6 µm³ were previously unrealistic. Reliability and speed must improve together, while still allowing even higher resolution on smaller volumes for cell biology.
ocar.action: Xu, Hayworth, Lu, Grob, Hassan, García-Cerdán, Niyogi, Nogales, Weinberg, and Hess present in eLife (2017) techniques that accelerate FIB-SEM acquisition and greatly improve reliability, allowing months of operation and continuously imaged volumes greater than 10^6 µm³, with examples from mammalian neural tissue, Drosophila brain, and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
ocar.resolution: The enhanced systems are described as large enough for connectomics, where excellent z-resolution can aid tracing of small neurites and speed human proofreading, while smaller volumes can be imaged at still higher resolution for cell biology.
ocar.future_work: The paper positions the platform for both connectomic volumes and high-resolution cell-biology volumes; using it for complete circuit reconstructions is the implied application.

summaries.beginner: A microscope that shaves and photographs tissue in extremely fine layers makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to be slow and prone to breaking during long runs. This work makes that microscope faster and stable enough to run for months, covering volumes useful for brain mapping.
summaries.intermediate: Xu et al. in eLife (2017) enhance FIB-SEM speed and reliability for months-long operation and continuously imaged volumes >10^6 µm³. They argue these volumes suit connectomics because high z-resolution helps trace small processes and reduces proofreading, with still higher resolution available on smaller volumes. Example datasets include mammalian neural tissue, Drosophila brain, and C. reinhardtii.
summaries.advanced: Volume >10^6 µm³ is a platform capability, not a finished connectome. Speed-up factors versus prior FIB-SEM are not numeric in the abstract (contrast Lu et al. 2019’s eight-fold claim). Fly is one example organism among three. Catalog method tags (enhanced long-run FIB-SEM) match.

plain_language_summary: A microscope that shaves and photographs tissue in extremely fine layers makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to be slow and prone to breaking during long runs. This work makes that microscope faster and stable enough to run for months, covering volumes useful for brain mapping.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing circuits from volume EM requires tracing entire neurons, but automated methods have error rates too high for reliable diagrams without extensive human proofreading. A method that greatly lengthens error-free neurite runs would cut that labor.
ocar.challenge: Standard convolutional segmentation lacks an iterative, object-centric memory for growing a single process. Any recurrent alternative must still run on SBEM-scale data (here zebra finch) without exploding merge rates, despite higher computational cost.
ocar.action: Januszewski, Kornfeld, Li, Pope, Blakely, Lindsey, Maitin-Shepard, Tyka, Denk, and Jain present flood-filling networks in Nature Methods (2017/catalog year): CNNs plus a recurrent pathway that iteratively extends individual neuronal processes, applied to zebra finch SBEM.
ocar.resolution: They report a mean error-free neurite path length of 1.1 mm and only four mergers in a 97 mm test set—an order of magnitude better than previous approaches on this dataset, though with substantially increased computational costs.
ocar.future_work: Reduced proofreading need is the stated payoff; the computational-cost increase implies hardware and runtime engineering as the practical next constraint.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace nerve cells in 3D pictures usually make too many breaks and false joins, so people spend years fixing them. This method grows each cell a bit at a time and, on a bird-brain test, went much farther without mistakes—at the price of needing more computation.
summaries.intermediate: Januszewski et al. in Nature Methods (2017) introduce flood-filling networks: convolutional nets with a recurrent pathway that iteratively extends neuronal processes. On zebra finch serial block-face EM they report 1.1 mm mean error-free path length and four mergers in 97 mm of test path, about 10× better than prior methods on the same dataset. Computational cost is substantially higher, traded against reduced proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Metrics are for this songbird SBEM test set; they should not be assumed for anisotropic serial-section mammalian cortex. Four mergers / 97 mm and 1.1 mm mean error-free length are the abstract’s headline numbers. Cost is acknowledged as substantially increased. Catalog dataset DS19 songbird matches.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace nerve cells in 3D pictures usually make too many breaks and false joins, so people spend years fixing them. This method grows each cell a bit at a time and, on a bird-brain test, went much farther without mistakes—at the price of needing more computation.

ocar.opportunity: Insects share developmental, organizational, and circuit features with vertebrates, so Drosophila is a powerful system for mechanistic behavior. Light-microscopy driver lines, activity tools, and emerging EM connectomes together could yield a whole-brain wiring diagram linked to function—if data can be integrated.
ocar.challenge: A larval whole-brain connectome from manual EM reconstruction was approaching completion, but an adult whole-brain dataset, already public, would take about 500–5000 person-years to reconstruct fully by hand (40× larval volume). Light, EM, physiology, and databases were siloed.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Costa, and Jefferis review in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017) available Drosophila data and tools, the status of larval versus adult EM, and the need to integrate light and EM with functional information. They argue rapid imaging and especially automated segmentation will likely deliver a complete adult connectome within about five years.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys resources and predicts an adult whole-brain connectome on a five-year horizon, while stressing FAIR-style integration so circuit-level behavior can be interpreted. They also consider limits of progress and implications for larger insects and vertebrates.
ocar.future_work: Integration of modalities into comprehensive databases, and automated segmentation to escape thousand-person-year manual adult reconstruction, are the explicit next requirements.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies already have genetic tools and, increasingly, detailed wiring maps. This review explains how combining photos, electron-microscope maps, and activity measurements could explain behavior—and why finishing the adult map by hand would take centuries of people-time.
summaries.intermediate: Schlegel, Costa, and Jefferis in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017) review Drosophila resources: large LM datasets, driver lines, activity tools, a near-complete larval EM connectome, and a public adult whole-brain EM volume. They estimate ~500–5000 person-years for fully manual adult reconstruction (40× larval volume) and predict automated segmentation could yield a complete adult connectome in ~5 years. They urge integrating light, EM, and physiology into databases.
summaries.advanced: The 500–5000 person-year range and 5-year prediction are 2017 estimates. This is a review, not a connectome release. Catalog tags (segmentation, infrastructure, fly, volume EM) match the topic. Later whole-brain efforts are outside this abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies already have genetic tools and, increasingly, detailed wiring maps. This review explains how combining photos, electron-microscope maps, and activity measurements could explain behavior—and why finishing the adult map by hand would take centuries of people-time.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical neuropil contains about 1 synapse per µm³, so dense mapping of even small blocks requires identifying millions to billions of synapses, of which about 80–90% are excitatory. As neurite reconstruction improves, synapse detection becomes the limiting step for dense connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse annotation does not scale. The method must work on conventionally en-bloc stained 3D EM, classify borders between processes as synaptic or not, and remain accurate enough for binary excitatory connectomes without user interaction.
ocar.action: Staffler, Berning, Boergens, Gour, van der Smagt, and Helmstaedter present SynEM in eLife (2017): automated detection of excitatory synapses from conventionally stained 3D EM, based on a segmentation and classification of neuronal-process borders.
ocar.resolution: SynEM yields 98% precision and recall in binary excitatory cortical connectomes with no user interaction, and is described as scaling to large cortical neuropil, plausibly even whole-brain datasets, removing the burden of manual synapse annotation for large dense maps.
ocar.future_work: Extension beyond excitatory cortical synapses and truly whole-brain scale is described as plausible rather than demonstrated; those are the stated frontiers.

summaries.beginner: A small cube of cortex contains millions of connections, too many to mark by hand. This method teaches a computer to decide which touching cell borders are real connections, and the authors report it is accurate enough to skip manual checking for excitatory maps.
summaries.intermediate: Staffler et al. in eLife (2017) introduce SynEM for automated excitatory-synapse detection on conventional en-bloc 3D EM. After segmentation, borders between processes are classified as synaptic or not. They report 98% precision and recall on binary excitatory cortical connectomes with no user interaction, arguing the method scales to large neuropil and plausibly whole-brain volumes.
summaries.advanced: 98% precision and recall apply to binary excitatory cortical connectomes as stated—not all synapse types (inhibitory, neuromodulatory). “No user interaction” is for this detection stage, assuming a segmentation. Whole-brain scaling is explicitly “plausible.” Catalog mentions Large-volume en-bloc staining (rOTO) as method context.

plain_language_summary: A small cube of cortex contains millions of connections, too many to mark by hand. This method teaches a computer to decide which touching cell borders are real connections, and the authors report it is accurate enough to skip manual checking for excitatory maps.

ocar.opportunity: Associating stimuli with reinforcement is essential for survival, but a complete synaptic wiring diagram of a higher-order associative-memory circuit had not been available. The Drosophila larval mushroom body was an attainable complete target.
ocar.challenge: How Kenyon cells mix projection-neuron inputs, how compartments implement a canonical motif, and how output neurons interact were incompletely known—including possible random versus stereotyped input, recurrent KC connections, and unanticipated modulatory synapses.
ocar.action: Eichler, Li, Litwin-Kumar, Park, Andrade, Schneider-Mizell, Saumweber, Huser, Eschbach, Gerber, Fetter, Truman, Priebe, Abbott, Thum, Zlatic, and Cardona reconstruct the Drosophila larval mushroom body at synaptic resolution (Nature, catalog year 2017).
ocar.resolution: Most Kenyon cells integrate random input combinations, but a subset receives stereotyped single-projection-neuron inputs; this organization maximizes a model output neuron’s stimulus-discrimination performance. Each compartment has a novel canonical circuit: reciprocal KC–modulatory neuron connections, modulatory-to-output connections, and many recurrent KC–KC synapses. Stereotyped connections among output neurons could enhance selection of learned behaviours.
ocar.future_work: The complete map is offered to guide future functional studies of this learning and memory centre.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring diagram of a fly larva’s learning center had been missing. Mapping every cell and contact, the authors found a mix of random and highly specific inputs, plus extra loops between cells that learning models had not fully included.
summaries.intermediate: Eichler et al. in Nature (2017) reconstruct the complete Drosophila larval mushroom body. Most KCs combine random PN inputs; a subset gets stereotyped single-PN input, which in a model maximizes discrimination by an output neuron. They report reciprocal KC–modulatory synapses, modulatory→output synapses, surprisingly many KC–KC recurrences, and stereotyped output–output connections that could aid selecting learned behaviors.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” is for this larval MB circuit, not the whole larva. Random versus stereotyped input is a reported mix, not 100% random. Discrimination maximization is a model result. Catalog has empty method tags; imaging modality is not named in the abstract (larval EM is implied by the reconstruction). DS03 Drosophila larva matches.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring diagram of a fly larva’s learning center had been missing. Mapping every cell and contact, the authors found a mix of random and highly specific inputs, plus extra loops between cells that learning models had not fully included.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping connectomes requires fast, accurate annotation of 3D EM. If trained crowds could reconstruct axons and dendrites much faster than with existing tools, the range of realistic connectomes would expand.
