ocar.challenge: Desktop annotation tools were too slow for mammalian cortical volumes. An in-browser, egocentric “flight mode” must stay usable on 3D EM while supporting crowd reconstruction at high path-length rates.
ocar.action: Boergens, Berning, Bocklisch, Bräunlein, Drawitsch, Frohnhofen, Herold, Otto, Rzepka, Werkmeister, Werner, Wiese, Wissler, and Helmstaedter present webKnossos in Nature Methods (2017): an in-browser 3D EM annotation tool with flight mode.
ocar.resolution: Trained annotator crowds reconstruct at 1.5 ± 0.6 mm/h for axons and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h for dendrites in mammalian cortical 3D EM. webKnossos is reported to accelerate neurite reconstruction 4- to 13-fold versus then-current state-of-the-art tools.
ocar.future_work: Faster crowd reconstruction extends which connectomes can be mapped; combining flight mode with improved automated segmentation is the implied complementary path.

summaries.beginner: Tracing branches in a 3D brain picture in a web browser, as if flying along them, lets trained people work much faster. This tool is reported to speed that tracing several-fold on mammalian cortex data.
summaries.intermediate: Boergens et al. in Nature Methods (2017) introduce webKnossos, an in-browser 3D EM annotator with egocentric flight mode. In mammalian cortex they report crowd speeds of 1.5 ± 0.6 mm/h (axons) and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h (dendrites). That is a 4- to 13-fold acceleration versus then-current tools, argued to widen feasible connectome scale.
summaries.advanced: Speeds are for trained crowds on mammalian cortical 3D EM; untrained users and other tissues may differ. The 4- to 13-fold range depends on the unnamed baseline tools. Flight mode is skeleton-style reconstruction, not volumetric proofreading of automated segmentation. Volume-EM method tag matches.

plain_language_summary: Tracing branches in a 3D brain picture in a web browser, as if flying along them, lets trained people work much faster. This tool is reported to speed that tracing several-fold on mammalian cortex data.

ocar.opportunity: Dense reconstructions of neuronal populations are critical for cell-type and circuit analysis, and require ultrastructural resolution throughout large volumes. A nearly complete map of neurons in a larval zebrafish olfactory bulb would enable morphological, geometric, and topological circuit analyses and public reuse.
ocar.challenge: Automated volumetric EM must be paired with conductive embedding (for SBEM), manual tracing, efficient error correction, and usable software for browsing, tracing, synapses, and visualization—plus sharing of raw data.
ocar.action: Wanner, Genoud, and Friedrich acquire an SBEM stack of a zebrafish larva olfactory bulb at 9.25 × 9.25 × 25 nm³ with conductive embedding, manually trace and error-correct skeletons of 1,022 neurons (98% of OB neurons), and release PyKNOSSOS for browsing, tracing, synapse annotation, and visualization, with data via neurodata.io.
ocar.resolution: The reconstructions support detailed morphology, projection, and subcellular analyses and dense geometrical/topological study of OB circuitry. Image data are accessible through neurodata web services; raw data and reconstructions can be visualized in PyKNOSSOS.
ocar.future_work: The resource is offered for further morphological and circuit analyses; remaining 2% of neurons and full synapse annotation beyond skeletons are natural extensions.

summaries.beginner: Researchers imaged a young zebrafish’s smell center in 3D at nanometer detail and traced nearly every nerve cell in it. They also share software and the pictures so others can study the same map.
summaries.intermediate: Wanner, Genoud, and Friedrich in Scientific Data (2016) report SBEM of a zebrafish larval olfactory bulb (9.25×9.25×25 nm³) with conductive embedding and skeletons of 1,022 neurons—98% of OB neurons—via manual tracing and error correction. They introduce PyKNOSSOS and share images through neurodata.io. The dense set enables morphological and topological circuit analyses.
summaries.advanced: 98% completeness is of OB neurons in this larva, not the whole brain. Voxel size is anisotropic (25 nm z). Skeletons are not a full volumetric synapse-resolved connectome unless synapses were fully annotated (software supports annotation; completeness of synapses is not claimed here). Catalog DS15 zebrafish matches.

plain_language_summary: Researchers imaged a young zebrafish’s smell center in 3D at nanometer detail and traced nearly every nerve cell in it. They also share software and the pictures so others can study the same map.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical circuits contain thousands of neurons and millions of synapses; relating activity to the underlying excitatory network in mouse visual cortex required pairing physiology with large-scale EM. A consensus that similarly tuned layer 2/3 pyramids excite each other still lacked an anatomical basis.
ocar.challenge: Light methods cannot resolve the dense local network. Even if axons and dendrites of all orientation selectivities pass near each other, one must determine whether synapses are specific at spine scale and whether synapse size further biases the network.
ocar.action: Lee, Bonin, Reed, Graham, Hood, Glattfelder, and Reid combine physiological imaging with large-scale electron microscopy in Nature (2016) to study an excitatory network in mouse V1, relating orientation selectivity to synaptic connectivity among layer 2/3 pyramids.
ocar.resolution: Layer 2/3 neurons organized into subnetworks with more connections within than between groups. Pyramids with similar orientation selectivity preferentially synapsed despite near-equal proximity (<5 μm) of axons and dendrites of all selectivities, and similar-tuning pairs also formed larger synapses. They predict specificity mechanisms act at spine length scale.
ocar.future_work: Functional connectomics of thousands of connections in one circuit is presented as a way to uncover cortical organizational logic; extending beyond this excitatory V1 patch is implied.

summaries.beginner: In mouse visual cortex, cells that like the same line orientation tend to talk to each other. By first measuring those preferences and then mapping the actual contacts with an electron microscope, this study shows the preference is real and not just because wires pass nearby.
summaries.intermediate: Lee et al. in Nature (2016) combine in vivo functional imaging with large-scale EM of mouse V1. Layer 2/3 pyramids form anatomically defined subnetworks; similarly orientation-selective cells preferentially synapse even though axons and dendrites of all selectivities pass within <5 μm with roughly equal probability. Similarly tuned pairs also make larger synapses, potentially amplifying specificity.
summaries.advanced: Results are for this excitatory L2/3 V1 network, not all cortical layers or inhibitory connections. The <5 μm proximity argument supports spine-scale specificity but does not identify the developmental mechanism. “Larger synapses” is reported without a numeric effect size in the abstract. Mouse organism tag matches; no registry dataset is named.

plain_language_summary: In mouse visual cortex, cells that like the same line orientation tend to talk to each other. By first measuring those preferences and then mapping the actual contacts with an electron microscope, this study shows the preference is real and not just because wires pass nearby.

ocar.opportunity: After neuron shapes are segmented, listing synapses can consume more than half of reconstruction effort, and that fraction will grow as segmentation improves. Fully automatic presynaptic detection plus postsynaptic partner assignment would ungate connectome speed, especially because contact area alone is not a sufficient predictor of a synapse.
ocar.challenge: Synapse annotation has lagged neuron tracing. Polyadic insect synapses, limited training data, and the need to evaluate on connectomes of meaningful size—not just small patches—make the problem harder. Methods should leverage improving segmentations directly.
ocar.action: Huang, Scheffer, and Plaza detect presynaptic structures with a U-Net CNN and postsynaptic partners with a multilayer perceptron whose features are conditioned on local segmentation, requiring minimal training, and introduce metrics for large connectomes, applying the system to Drosophila EM.
ocar.resolution: On Drosophila EM, their metrics indicate a completely automatic prediction can characterize most connectivity correctly, providing a complete solution for polyadic synapse detection in this setting.
ocar.future_work: Remaining errors still matter for rare edges; the authors emphasize evaluation on large connectomes as the right test, implying further partner-error analysis on full graphs.

summaries.beginner: Once cell shapes are drawn, marking every contact can take as much work as the drawing did. This paper trains computers to find the sending side of a contact and then its receiving partners, and reports that most of the wiring in a fly dataset can be recovered automatically.
summaries.intermediate: Huang, Scheffer, and Plaza in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2016) use a U-Net for presynaptic detection and a segmentation-conditioned MLP for postsynaptic partners, aiming at polyadic synapses with little training data. They introduce evaluation metrics at connectome scale. Fully automatic predictions on Drosophila EM are reported to characterize most connectivity correctly, underscoring that contact area alone is not enough.
summaries.advanced: “Most of the connectivity correctly” is not a numeric precision/recall in the abstract. Success is on Drosophila EM (spelling “Drosphila” in the source abstract). Catalog year 2016 vs journal appearance 2018 in some indexes; venue here is Front. Neural Circuits. Partner MLP depends on local segmentation quality.

plain_language_summary: Once cell shapes are drawn, marking every contact can take as much work as the drawing did. This paper trains computers to find the sending side of a contact and then its receiving partners, and reports that most of the wiring in a fly dataset can be recovered automatically.

ocar.opportunity: Serial EM can yield not only who connects to whom but vesicle types, how many partners sit at a presynaptic site, and how inputs and outputs are arranged on arbors. Two leech ganglion volumes—one a neuropil sample, one an entire juvenile ganglion—could place mature ultrastructure in the context of complete arbors.
ocar.challenge: Partial neuropil reconstructions cannot show whether arbors segregate input-only versus mixed zones. Criteria for identifying synapses and counting postsynaptic partners at boutons must be defined on real data, then applied to fully reconstructed neurons including somata.
ocar.action: Pipkin, Bushong, Ellisman, and Kristan collect two serial block-face SEM volumes from medicinal leech ganglia: a small adult neuropil sample and an entire juvenile ganglion. They measure vesicle-containing arbors, develop synapse criteria, count apparent postsynaptic partners, and map spatial distributions of inputs and outputs on complete arbors.
ocar.resolution: Some neurons segregate arbors into input-only and mixed input/output zones; others have exclusively mixed zones; still others only input zones. These patterns are offered as groundwork for behavioral studies.
ocar.future_work: Relating these arbor polarity patterns to behavior is explicitly left for future work.

summaries.beginner: In a leech nerve cluster, some cells only receive messages on parts of their branches, some both send and receive in the same places, and some only receive. Mapping two 3D electron-microscope volumes revealed those layouts.
summaries.intermediate: Pipkin et al. in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2016) analyze two SBEM volumes from Hirudo: a fraction of adult neuropil and an entire juvenile ganglion. They classify vesicle types, define synapse criteria, and count postsynaptic partners at boutons, then map input/output zones on complete arbors. Neurons fall into segregated input-versus-mixed, mixed-only, or input-only arbor classes.
summaries.advanced: Partner counts are “apparent” appositions. Adult neuropil is a sample, not a complete adult ganglion; complete arbors are from the juvenile. Behavioral links are prospective. SEM/SBEM tags match.

plain_language_summary: In a leech nerve cluster, some cells only receive messages on parts of their branches, some both send and receive in the same places, and some only receive. Mapping two 3D electron-microscope volumes revealed those layouts.

ocar.opportunity: Cajal established neurons as structural units, but sample preparation, imaging, and computation were insufficient for mapping an entire mammalian brain with all neurons and connections. Mesoscopic tracing and MRI-DTI give partial maps; a cellular whole-brain connectome still appeared newly reachable.
ocar.challenge: Sparse labeling aligned to atlases and diffusion MRI do not yield complete connectivity of an individual brain. Large-volume EM acquisition and automated neurite reconstruction remain substantial obstacles even as whole-brain preparation and high-throughput EM advance.
ocar.action: Mikula’s Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2016) perspective reviews the status of mammalian whole-brain cellular connectomics, arguing that recent whole-brain sample preparation and high-throughput EM put the goal within reach, while cataloguing remaining acquisition and reconstruction obstacles, and calling for a concerted attack on a small mammalian whole brain.
ocar.resolution: The piece concludes that the time is right to launch a concerted connectomic effort on a small mammalian whole brain, with cellular resolution rather than mesoscale proxies.
ocar.future_work: The remaining obstacles named—large-volume EM and automated neurite reconstruction—are the agenda for that concerted effort.

summaries.beginner: We still do not have a complete cell-by-cell wiring diagram of any mammal’s whole brain. This perspective argues that new ways to prepare and photograph an entire small-mammal brain make it time to try.
summaries.intermediate: Mikula in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2016) contrasts Cajal-era limits with mesoscopic projection atlases and MRI-DTI, which cannot deliver complete individual connectivity. He argues whole-brain preparation plus high-throughput EM now make mammalian cellular connectomics reachable, while large-volume acquisition and automated reconstruction remain hard. He urges a concerted project on a small mammalian whole brain.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a dataset. “Within reach” is a 2016 judgment. Volume EM method tag matches the topic; no specific organism beyond mammal is named in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: We still do not have a complete cell-by-cell wiring diagram of any mammal’s whole brain. This perspective argues that new ways to prepare and photograph an entire small-mammal brain make it time to try.

ocar.opportunity: Brain left–right asymmetries are usually minor or cryptic. The tiny dorsal tubular CNS of the Ciona intestinalis tadpole larva—a chordate with a well-studied early neural development but unreported cellular organization in the swimming larva—offered a complete synaptic connectome in which sidedness could be scored cell by cell.
ocar.challenge: Equal cell numbers on left and right might still hide different identities and pathways. Capturing chemical synapses, neuromuscular junctions, gap junctions, polyadic and reciprocal motifs, and ciliary organelles across the whole larval CNS requires serial-section EM of all 177 CNS neurons.
ocar.action: Ryan, Lu, and Meinertzhagen document in eLife (2016) the synaptic connectome of the larva’s 177 CNS neurons from serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: These neurons formed 6618 synapses including 1772 neuromuscular junctions, plus 1206 gap junctions. Neurons are unipolar with at most a single dendrite and few synapses; 922 synapses were polyadic; axo-axonal synapses predominate. Despite equal cell numbers, identities and pathways differ left/right; brain-vesicle asymmetries include a right ocellus and left coronet cells.
ocar.future_work: The map highlights chordate brain sidedness at cellular resolution; functional tests of asymmetric pathways are outside this anatomy paper.

summaries.beginner: A sea-squirt tadpole has only 177 nerve cells in its central nervous system, so every connection can be listed. The two sides have the same number of cells but not the same identities or pathways, including a light-sensing structure on the right.
summaries.intermediate: Ryan, Lu, and Meinertzhagen in eLife (2016) reconstruct the Ciona intestinalis tadpole larval CNS: 177 neurons, 6618 chemical synapses (1772 NMJs), and 1206 gap junctions. Neurons are unipolar with few synapses; 922 synapses are polyadic; axo-axonal contacts predominate. Left and right differ in neuron identity and pathways despite equal counts, with a right ocellus and left coronet cells among brain-vesicle asymmetries.
summaries.advanced: Counts are for this larva’s reconstruction. “Few synapses” and unipolar morphology are species-specific and should not be generalized to vertebrates. Catalog DS20 Ciona matches. Functional navigation roles of asymmetries are not shown here.

plain_language_summary: A sea-squirt tadpole has only 177 nerve cells in its central nervous system, so every connection can be listed. The two sides have the same number of cells but not the same identities or pathways, including a light-sensing structure on the right.

ocar.opportunity: Smell lets animals respond to long-distance cues via learned and innate valences, but how the first olfactory neuropil implements gain control, integration, and salience was incomplete without a complete EM wiring diagram. The Drosophila larval antennal lobe, analogous to the vertebrate olfactory bulb, was fully mappable.
ocar.challenge: Uniglomerular versus multiglomerular projection paths, local-neuron hierarchy, and putative bistable gain control (panglomerular inhibition versus detecting faint aversive odors amid strong appetitive ones) required every synapse among ORNs, LNs, and PNs.
ocar.action: Berck, Khandelwal, Claus, Hernandez-Nunez, Si, Tabone, Li, Truman, Fetter, Louis, Samuel, and Cardona map with EM the complete wiring diagram of the Drosophila larval antennal lobe (bioRxiv 2016).
ocar.resolution: They find a canonical circuit in which uniglomerular PNs relay gain-controlled ORN activity to mushroom body and lateral horn, plus a parallel mPN/LN circuit that integrates multiple ORN signals at the first synapse. LN–LN connections putatively implement bistable gain control. The complete diagram is offered to bridge circuits and behavior.
ocar.future_work: Experimental and theoretical studies using this map to test the bistable-gain and integration hypotheses are explicitly invited.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly larva’s first smell station was mapped contact by contact. The map shows one path that reports single smell channels and another that mixes channels, with local cells that may switch how the system balances strong and faint smells.
summaries.intermediate: Berck et al. on bioRxiv (2016) reconstruct the complete Drosophila larval antennal lobe. Uniglomerular PNs relay gain-controlled ORN activity to MB and lateral horn; a parallel mPN and hierarchical LN circuit integrates multiple ORNs at the first synapse. LN–LN synapses are proposed to switch between panglomerular inhibition (saliency) and allowing faint aversive glomeruli through during strong appetitive odors.
summaries.advanced: Bistable gain control is putatively inferred from LN–LN anatomy, not physiology in this paper. Completeness is for this glomerular olfactory system, not the whole larva. DS03 Drosophila larva matches. Bridging to behavior is prospective.

plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly larva’s first smell station was mapped contact by contact. The map shows one path that reports single smell channels and another that mixes channels, with local cells that may switch how the system balances strong and faint smells.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping connections among hundreds or thousands of densely packed neurons needs volume EM with synaptic resolution and a large field of view. Microtome-based serial block-face SEM is a leading candidate for circuit reconstruction, but neuroscience use poses extreme demands on resolution, FOV, time, and sample preparation—and then on terabyte-scale analysis.
ocar.challenge: SBEM, ssTEM, ATUM, and FIB-SEM each trade resolution, speed, and reliability. Dense reconstruction of microcircuits remains largely missing. SBEM-specific challenges (charging, cutting, staining) and the lack of mature image-processing pipelines for terabyte stacks limit circuit reconstruction.
ocar.action: Wanner, Kirschmann, and Genoud review in Journal of Microscopy (2015) SBEM challenges for neuroscience circuit reconstruction, comparing volume-EM techniques and surveying image-processing and analysis pipelines for terabyte-scale data, with recent SBEM advances for circuit work.
ocar.resolution: The review positions SBEM among volume-EM methods that can resolve synapses and support dense reconstruction, while emphasizing remaining acquisition and analysis bottlenecks and available workflows.
ocar.future_work: New image-processing workflows for terabyte SBEM are presented as still needed as datasets grow.

summaries.beginner: One way to photograph a 3D chunk of brain is to shave the surface of a block inside an electron microscope, again and again. This review explains why that is powerful for wiring diagrams and why sample prep, imaging time, and huge files still make it hard.
summaries.intermediate: Wanner, Kirschmann, and Genoud in Journal of Microscopy (2015) review microtome-based serial block-face SEM for circuit reconstruction. They compare SBEM with ssTEM, ATUM, and FIB-SEM on resolution, field of view, time, and preparation, and discuss terabyte-scale analysis pipelines. Circuit reconstruction is framed as a main driver of SBEM development.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review, not a connectome. Tradeoffs are qualitative in the abstract. Catalog methods SBF-SEM and ssTEM match the comparison set.

plain_language_summary: One way to photograph a 3D chunk of brain is to shave the surface of a block inside an electron microscope, again and again. This review explains why that is powerful for wiring diagrams and why sample prep, imaging time, and huge files still make it hard.

ocar.opportunity: Dense connectomic mapping is limited by the time needed to analyze 3D EM; automated segmentation error rates force heavy manual correction. Any change that lowers those error rates would directly speed analysis. Preserving extracellular space during chemical fixation might make neurites easier to separate and synapses easier to identify.
ocar.challenge: Standard fixation collapses extracellular space, crowding membranes. Algorithms then merge processes; electrical synapses are hard to see; and antibody penetration for correlated light/EM is poor without harsh permeabilization.
ocar.action: Pallotto, Watkins, Fubara, Singer, and Briggman preserve extracellular space during chemical fixation (eLife 2015) and test effects on machine-learning segmentation, electrical-synapse identification, and antibody penetration with only minimal permeabilization.
ocar.resolution: ECS-preserved tissue is easier to segment with ML algorithms, with significantly reduced error rates; electrical synapses are readily identified; and antibodies penetrate deeply with minimal permeabilization, enabling correlated LM/EM. They conclude ECS preservation benefits multiple aspects of connectomic analysis.
ocar.future_work: Adopting ECS-preserving fixation in production connectomic pipelines is the implied next step from these demonstrated benefits.

summaries.beginner: Usual chemical fixation squishes the gaps between brain cells, making them harder for computers to tell apart. Keeping those gaps open, this study finds, helps automatic tracing, reveals a class of tight junctions, and lets stains soak in more easily.
summaries.intermediate: Pallotto et al. in eLife (2015) preserve extracellular space during chemical fixation. Machine-learning segmentation error rates fall significantly; electrical synapses become readily identifiable; antibodies penetrate deep with only minimal permeabilization, supporting correlated light and EM. They argue ECS preservation aids connectomic analysis on several fronts.
summaries.advanced: “Significantly reduced” error rates are not given numerically in the abstract. ECS preservation can trade off against other ultrastructural goals (the abstract does not discuss them). Organism is unspecified. Method tag ECS-preserving fixation matches.

plain_language_summary: Usual chemical fixation squishes the gaps between brain cells, making them harder for computers to tell apart. Keeping those gaps open, this study finds, helps automatic tracing, reveals a class of tight junctions, and lets stains soak in more easily.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale connectomics requires dense EM staining of sizable tissue blocks. Prior en-bloc protocols produced staining gradients that substantially limited reconstructable 3D volumes, blocking correlated functional and structural work that needs less precise topographic targeting.
ocar.challenge: Stain penetration into millimeter-scale mammalian cortex is uneven; gradients leave interiors unusable for dense reconstruction. A protocol that densely stains mouse neocortex blocks at least 1 mm in diameter would relax targeting constraints.
ocar.action: Hua, Laserstein, and Helmstaedter report in Nature Communications (2015) a large-volume dense en-bloc EM staining protocol (rOTO-style) that overcomes staining gradients.
ocar.resolution: The protocol provides densely reconstructable mouse neocortex blocks at least 1 mm in diameter, making correlated functional and structural circuit analysis more realistic by relaxing precise topographic sample targeting.
ocar.future_work: Using these uniformly stained millimeter blocks for combined physiology and EM is the stated enabling goal.

summaries.beginner: To map a cubic millimeter of cortex, the whole piece must take up stain evenly, or the middle is unreadable. This recipe stains mouse cortex blocks at least a millimeter across without the usual fade toward the center.
summaries.intermediate: Hua, Laserstein, and Helmstaedter in Nature Communications (2015) introduce a large-volume dense en-bloc EM staining protocol that overcomes staining gradients. They report densely reconstructable mouse neocortex blocks at least 1 mm in diameter. Relaxed topographic targeting is meant to make correlated functional and structural circuit analyses more realistic.
summaries.advanced: “At least 1 mm in diameter” is the size claim; isotropy of stain through the full depth should be read from the full methods, not the abstract alone. This is a staining protocol, not a completed millimeter connectome. Mouse neocortex is the demonstrated tissue.

plain_language_summary: To map a cubic millimeter of cortex, the whole piece must take up stain evenly, or the middle is unreadable. This recipe stains mouse cortex blocks at least a millimeter across without the usual fade toward the center.

ocar.opportunity: EM circuit mapping usually demands laborious proofreading or reconciling multiple independent reconstructions. Quantitative arbor and network context might let iterative reconstruction replace redundant effort, if one knew how morphology relates to connectivity errors.
ocar.challenge: Most synapses sit on small microtubule-free twigs off a backbone; omitting twigs might dominate errors, yet strong connections might be distributed across twigs and thus robust to missing one. Measuring that in Drosophila sensorimotor (larva) and visual (adult) systems required new reconstructions plus existing ones.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell, Gerhard, Longair, Kazimiers, Li, Zwart, Champion, Midgley, Fetter, Saalfeld, and Cardona develop quantitative arbor and network methods to iteratively proofread and reconstruct Drosophila circuits (bioRxiv 2015), measuring morphological underpinnings of connectivity in larval sensorimotor and adult visual systems.
ocar.resolution: Synaptic inputs preferentially occupy numerous small microtubule-free twigs; omitting individual twigs accounted for 96% of errors. Synapses of highly connected neurons were distributed across multiple twigs, so strong connections were robust to reconstruction error. Iterative reconstruction matched the consensus of multiple reconstructions, overcoming the need for redundant effort.
ocar.future_work: Applying these morphology–connectivity rules to larger fly volumes is the implied generalization.

summaries.beginner: Most fly-neuron mistakes happen when a computer misses tiny side twigs where many contacts sit. Because important connections usually use several twigs, a careful checking method can skip tracing every cell three times and still get the strong wiring right.
summaries.intermediate: Schneider-Mizell et al. (bioRxiv 2015; eLife catalog DOI) introduce iterative, anatomy-aware proofreading for Drosophila EM. Inputs lie mostly on microtubule-free twigs; 96% of errors were omitted twigs. High-degree connections spread across twigs, conferring robustness. Iterative reconstruction achieved consensus-level wiring without fully redundant independent traces, in larval sensorimotor and adult visual circuits.
summaries.advanced: 96% of errors being omitted twigs is specific to these reconstructions. Robustness applies to strong (highly connected) pairs, not weak edges. Comparison is iterative versus multi-reconstruction consensus. Fly / electron microscopy tags match.

plain_language_summary: Most fly-neuron mistakes happen when a computer misses tiny side twigs where many contacts sit. Because important connections usually use several twigs, a careful checking method can skip tracing every cell three times and still get the strong wiring right.

ocar.opportunity: A saturated reconstruction in which every axon, dendrite, glia, and many organelles in a neocortical sub-volume are itemized would let physical properties of tissue be measured directly and would test whether proximity predicts synapses (Peters’ rule).
ocar.challenge: Manual saturated reconstruction at nanometer resolution was historically impossible at even modest volumes. All cellular objects and subcellular components (synapses, vesicles, spines, spine apparati, PSDs, mitochondria) must be rendered into a minable database.
ocar.action: Kasthuri, Hayworth, Berger, Schalek, Conchello, Knowles-Barley, Lee, Vázquez-Reina, Kaynig, Jones, Roberts, Morgan, Tapia, Seung, Gray Roncal, Vogelstein, Burns, Sussman, Priebe, Pfister, and Lichtman describe automated technologies for nanometer-resolution structure and generate a saturated reconstruction of a mouse neocortex sub-volume (Cell 2015), tracing all excitatory axons and their synaptic and non-synaptic juxtapositions with every dendritic spine.
ocar.resolution: Physical proximity is not sufficient to predict synaptic connectivity, refuting Peters’ rule in this volume. The online minable database provides general access to neocortical complexity for further data-driven inquiries.
ocar.future_work: The database is explicitly offered for further inquiries; expanding saturated volumes remains limited by the same reconstruction cost.

summaries.beginner: In a small piece of mouse cortex, every cell process and many tiny parts were listed in a database. Following all the close passes between outgoing wires and spines showed that merely touching distance does not decide whether a connection exists.
summaries.intermediate: Kasthuri et al. in Cell (2015) present automated nanometer-resolution methods and a saturated reconstruction of a mouse neocortical sub-volume, itemizing axons, dendrites, glia, synapses, vesicles, spines, spine apparati, PSDs, and mitochondria. By scoring synaptic versus non-synaptic axon–spine juxtapositions they refute Peters’ rule that proximity predicts connectivity. Data are shared as an online minable database (DS11 Kasthuri neocortex).
summaries.advanced: Refutation of Peters’ rule is for this sub-volume’s excitatory axons and spines, not all brain regions. “Saturated” means all cellular objects in the reconstructed sub-volume, not a cortical column or whole brain. Catalog DS11 matches.

plain_language_summary: In a small piece of mouse cortex, every cell process and many tiny parts were listed in a database. Following all the close passes between outgoing wires and spines showed that merely touching distance does not decide whether a connection exists.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM can image neural tissue at below 10 × 10 × 10 nm, producing data suited to automatic connectome tracing, but samples thicker than a FIB-friendly chunk cannot be acquired as one run. Reliably subdividing embedded tissue and stitching volumes back would extend FIB-SEM to larger specimens.
ocar.challenge: Mechanical partitioning must remain ultrastructurally smooth so neurites can be traced across chunk boundaries. Chunks (~20 μm thick) must be mounted for efficient parallel FIB-SEM, then computationally volume-stitched into a tracing-ready 3D dataset.
ocar.action: Hayworth, Xu, Lu, Knott, Fetter, Tapia, Lichtman, and Hess present ultrathick sectioning (hot-knife partitioning) in Nature Methods (2015): embedded tissue is subdivided into ~20 μm chunks for parallel FIB-SEM, then volume-stitched.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produces a final three-dimensional dataset suitable for connectome tracing, described as a technical advance for larger-scale FIB-SEM connectomics.
ocar.future_work: Larger-scale parallel FIB-SEM of hot-knife chunks is the intended use; stitching quality on production brains is the practical sequel.

summaries.beginner: The best 3D electron microscopes can only chew through a thin slab at a time. This method slices stained brain into thicker, still-smooth pieces that can be imaged in parallel and then digitally glued back into one volume.
summaries.intermediate: Hayworth et al. in Nature Methods (2015) introduce ultrathick sectioning: embedded samples are split into ~20 μm chunks optimally sized for parallel FIB-SEM, then volume-stitched. They report ultrastructurally smooth partitions. The stitched 3D dataset is described as suitable for automatic connectome tracing at below 10 nm × 10 nm × 10 nm class FIB-SEM resolution.
summaries.advanced: 20 μm thickness and <10 nm voxel class are the abstract’s figures. Stitching suitability for tracing is claimed but alignment error rates are not given here. Hot-knife / FIB-SEM method tags match. Organism unspecified.

plain_language_summary: The best 3D electron microscopes can only chew through a thin slab at a time. This method slices stained brain into thicker, still-smooth pieces that can be imaged in parallel and then digitally glued back into one volume.

ocar.opportunity: Except for the C. elegans microscale connectome, complete connectivity datasets in other species were lacking. A brain-wide, cellular-level mesoscale map of the mouse would underpin local and global information-processing studies and provide a shared atlas for health and disease circuits.
ocar.challenge: Tracing every axon type across a whole mouse brain requires standardized labeling, whole-brain imaging, and registration into a common 3D space to build a connectivity matrix, plus models of strength, symmetry, and pathway organization.
ocar.action: Oh, Harris, Ng, Winslow, Cain, Mihalas, Wang, Lau, Kuan, Henry, Mortrud, Ouellette, Nguyen, Sorensen, Slaughterbeck, Wakeman, Li, Feng, Ho, Nicholas, Hirokawa, Bohn, Joines, Peng, Hawrylycz, Phillips, Hohmann, Wohnoutka, Gerfen, Koch, Bernard, Dang, Jones, and Zeng report in Nature (2014) the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas: EGFP-expressing AAV tracing from defined regions and cell types, imaged by high-throughput serial two-photon tomography and registered to a common 3D reference, yielding a whole-brain connectivity matrix and computational analyses including cortico-thalamic pathways.
ocar.resolution: The atlas is a freely available foundational resource. A computational model yields insights into connectional strength distribution, symmetry, and other network properties; virtual tractography illustrates 3D topography; cortico-thalamic analysis demonstrates segregation and integration of parallel pathways.
ocar.future_work: The resource is intended for structural and functional investigations of circuits supporting behavior and cognition in health and disease.

summaries.beginner: Researchers injected glowing tracers into many mouse brain areas and photographed the whole brain, then lined up all the experiments in a shared 3D atlas. The result is a region-to-region wiring map for the mouse, released for anyone to use.
summaries.intermediate: Oh et al. in Nature (2014) present the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas: AAV-EGFP projection tracing from defined regions and cell types, serial two-photon tomography, and registration to a common 3D space, producing a brain-wide mesoscale connectivity matrix. Modeling addresses strength, symmetry, and network properties; virtual tractography and cortico-thalamic analyses show topography plus segregation/integration of parallel pathways. Data are freely available.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale (region/cell-type projections), not a synapse-resolution EM connectome; the abstract’s C. elegans contrast makes that scale difference explicit. Catalog tags listing elegans as organism contradict the mouse atlas—this annotation follows the abstract. Serial two-photon is the imaging method.

plain_language_summary: Researchers injected glowing tracers into many mouse brain areas and photographed the whole brain, then lined up all the experiments in a shared 3D atlas. The result is a region-to-region wiring map for the mouse, released for anyone to use.

ocar.opportunity: Animals use spatial light differences for visual navigation, but how light maps onto coordinated motor output was poorly understood. A complete 71-neuron, four-eye circuit in the Platynereis larva was small enough for serial-section TEM plus behavioral tests of phototaxis.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing photoreceptors through three interneuron layers to motorneurons innervating trunk muscles, then linking that anatomy to left–right light comparison, required both a full connectome and eye-ablation behavior. Contrast enhancement in the circuit also needed a mechanistic motif.
ocar.action: Randel, Asadulina, Bezares-Calderón, Verasztó, Williams, Conzelmann, Shahidi, and Jékely reconstruct the four-eye visual circuit of a Platynereis larva with serial-section TEM (eLife 2014) and combine eye ablations with behavioral experiments.
ocar.resolution: The 71-neuron circuit compares light on either side and stimulates bending upon left–right imbalance during phototaxis. An interneuron motif enhances sensitivity to intensity contrasts. The circuit shows spatial light detection and contrast modulation, illustrating how image-forming eyes might evolve via stages that only contrast light versus dark during a simple visual task.
ocar.future_work: The evolutionary intermediate-stage argument is interpretive; further comparative circuits could test it.

summaries.beginner: A marine worm larva with four simple eyes was mapped cell by cell. The wiring compares light on the left and right and bends the body toward or away from it, a stepping stone toward more camera-like vision.
summaries.intermediate: Randel et al. in eLife (2014) reconstruct a 71-neuron Platynereis larval visual circuit (photoreceptors, three interneuron layers, motorneurons to trunk muscle) with serial-section TEM. Combined with eye ablations, they show the circuit computes left–right light imbalance for phototaxis and includes an interneuron motif that enhances contrast sensitivity. They frame this as a visual system with spatial detection and contrast modulation.
summaries.advanced: n is one reconstructed circuit plus behavioral eye ablations; completeness is 71 neurons as stated. Evolution of image-forming eyes is a hypothesis illustrated by this circuit. Catalog DS22 Platynereis / TEM matches.

plain_language_summary: A marine worm larva with four simple eyes was mapped cell by cell. The wiring compares light on the left and right and bends the body toward or away from it, a stepping stone toward more camera-like vision.

ocar.opportunity: How the mammalian retina detects motion remained unsolved for 50 years. Reconstructing Off-type starburst amacrine cells and bipolar cells in serial EM, with help from the EyeWire community, could reveal whether bipolar types wire to SAC dendrites in a space-time-specific pattern that would create outward direction selectivity.
ocar.challenge: Contact area and branch depth must be scored at scale. Different bipolar types are known to differ in visual-response timing; mapping which type prefers near-soma versus far-soma SAC dendrites requires dense reconstruction plus a model linking anatomy to space–time receptive fields.
ocar.action: Kim, Greene, Zlateski, Lee, Richardson, Turaga, Purcaro, Balkam, Robinson, Behabadi, Campos, Denk, and Seung reconstruct Off SACs and bipolar cells in serial EM with EyeWire citizen scientists (Nature 2014), quantitatively analyzing contact area and retinal branch depth, then using a mathematical model of space–time wiring specificity.
ocar.resolution: One bipolar type prefers to wire near the SAC soma and another far from it; the near type is known to lag the far type in visual-response time. The model shows how this space–time wiring could give SAC dendrites receptive fields oriented in space–time and thus selective for stimuli moving outward from the soma.
ocar.future_work: The model predicts outward-selective SAC dendrites from anatomy plus known timing; physiological confirmation of that predicted RF is the natural test.

summaries.beginner: How the eye sees motion has been a puzzle for decades. Mapping cells in the mouse retina with help from online volunteers suggested that slower and faster incoming cells land at different places on a star-shaped neuron, which a model says would make that neuron prefer motion away from its center.
summaries.intermediate: Kim et al. in Nature (2014) reconstruct Off starburst amacrine cells and bipolar cells from serial EM with EyeWire crowd proofreading. Contact area and branch depth indicate one bipolar type prefers proximal SAC dendrites and another distal ones; the proximal type lags in time. A model shows space–time wiring specificity could confer outward direction selectivity on SAC dendrites.
summaries.advanced: This is anatomy plus a model, not a new in vivo SAC direction-selectivity recording in this paper. Timing differences are cited as known properties of the bipolar types. Off-type SACs/BCs only. DS09/DS10 mouse retina and EyeWire tags match.

plain_language_summary: How the eye sees motion has been a puzzle for decades. Mapping cells in the mouse retina with help from online volunteers suggested that slower and faster incoming cells land at different places on a star-shaped neuron, which a model says would make that neuron prefer motion away from its center.

ocar.opportunity: Analyzing neurons at scale usually means installing many tools and switching between analysis and visualization environments. An interoperable open-source R suite that reads local and remote data, visualizes, clusters, and compares morphology and connectivity after co-registration would lower that barrier, especially for Drosophila LM and EM datasets.
ocar.challenge: Most tools do not compare neurons across imaging modalities and template spaces. Bridging the majority of Drosophila light-microscopy and EM connectomic datasets in one environment is a software-integration problem.
ocar.action: Manton, Bates, Jagannathan, Costa, Schlegel, Rohlfing, and Jefferis present the natverse (bioRxiv; catalog year 2014): a suite of interoperable open-source R packages for reading data, visualization, clustering, graph-theoretic analysis of branching, co-registration, and transformations between template spaces and modalities, with tools integrating most Drosophila LM and EM datasets.
ocar.resolution: The natverse is described as an easy-to-use environment for large-scale neuroanatomical analysis and an open platform to create and share new packages.
ocar.future_work: Community extension of packages and continued ingestion of new fly datasets are the implied maintenance path.

summaries.beginner: Fly-brain researchers often juggle many programs to compare cell shapes. This toolbox in the R language is meant to read, draw, and compare those shapes—including mixing light-microscope and electron-microscope maps—in one place.
summaries.intermediate: Manton et al. (bioRxiv; catalog year 2014) introduce the natverse, interoperable R packages for neuroanatomy: local and remote input, visualization, clustering, graph analysis of branching, and comparison of morphology and connectivity after co-registration. They demonstrate integration of most Drosophila light-microscopy and EM connectomic datasets. The suite is offered as an open platform to create and share new packages.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year 2014 may not match later formal publication; this card uses the shard metadata. “Vast majority” of Drosophila datasets is the authors’ claim. R-centric by design. Alignment/infrastructure/fly tags match.

plain_language_summary: Fly-brain researchers often juggle many programs to compare cell shapes. This toolbox in the R language is meant to read, draw, and compare those shapes—including mixing light-microscope and electron-microscope maps—in one place.

ocar.opportunity: Local motion detection in the insect visual system remained elusive despite half a century of work, largely for lack of a synaptic connectome of the repeating medulla module. A semi-automated EM reconstruction could identify cell types in a motion circuit and test whether connections onto motion-sensitive neurons match their direction selectivity.
ocar.challenge: Assembling 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synapses in Drosophila optic medulla, matching them to light-microscopy types, and extracting the repeating module requires a pipeline that is only semi-automated, not fully hands-off.
ocar.action: Takemura, Bharioke, Lu, Nern, Vitaladevuni, Rivlin, Katz, Olbris, Plaza, Winston, Zhao, Horne, Fetter, Takemura, Blazek, Chang, Ogundeyi, Saunders, Shapiro, Sigmund, Rubin, Scheffer, Meinertzhagen, and Chklovskii develop a semi-automated EM pipeline (Nature 2013) to reconstruct a medulla connectome and match neurons to light-microscopy cell types.
ocar.resolution: Within the repeating module they identify cell types constituting a motion-detection circuit and show that connections onto individual motion-sensitive neurons were consistent with their direction selectivity. Results identify cellular targets for functional work and demonstrate that connectomes can provide key insights into neuronal computations.
ocar.future_work: Cellular targets are explicitly for future functional investigations of the motion circuit.

summaries.beginner: How a fly sees motion was still unsettled after decades. Mapping a repeating unit of the fly’s visual brain showed a set of cell types whose connections match the directions those cells prefer, pointing to which cells to test next.
summaries.intermediate: Takemura et al. in Nature (2013) reconstruct 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synapses in Drosophila optic medulla with a semi-automated EM pipeline, assign types by matching light microscopy, and assemble the repeating medulla module. They identify a motion-detection circuit whose inputs onto motion-sensitive neurons are consistent with direction selectivity. The map is meant to nominate cellular targets for functional work.
summaries.advanced: The connectome is a medulla module, not the whole visual system. Consistency with direction selectivity is anatomical, not a new physiology dataset in this paper. 379 neurons / 8,637 synapses are the headline counts. Fly / EM tags match.

plain_language_summary: How a fly sees motion was still unsettled after decades. Mapping a repeating unit of the fly’s visual brain showed a set of cell types whose connections match the directions those cells prefer, pointing to which cells to test next.

ocar.opportunity: Neuronal networks are high-dimensional graphs packed at extreme density, so comprehensively mapping them is a major challenge. Volume EM now makes data acquisition feasible for circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, but data analysis is massively lagging.
ocar.challenge: The perspective’s aim is to quantify analysis challenges in cellular-resolution connectomics: dense packing, error-prone automation, and the need for either huge human effort or better machine learning and crowdsourcing.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter in Nature Methods (2013) summarizes and quantifies challenges for data analysis in cellular-resolution connectomics and describes then-current solutions involving online crowd-sourcing and machine-learning approaches, given that volume EM acquisition for modest circuits had become feasible.
ocar.resolution: The perspective frames analysis—not acquisition—as the bottleneck for dense reconstructions of hundreds to thousands of neurons, and points to crowdsourcing plus ML as the available paths.
ocar.future_work: Closing the analysis lag relative to acquisition is the agenda the article sets.

summaries.beginner: Taking the pictures of a small circuit is now possible; turning those pictures into a reliable wiring list is the slow part. This commentary explains how hard that analysis is and how online volunteers and machine learning were being used to catch up.
summaries.intermediate: Helmstaedter in Nature Methods (2013) argues that volume EM can acquire circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, but analysis lags massively. He quantifies cellular-resolution connectomics analysis challenges. Current solutions discussed are online crowd-sourcing and machine-learning approaches.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a methods benchmark. Circuit-size feasibility is a 2013 snapshot. Volume EM / proofreading / graph-analysis tags match the topic. No organism specified.

plain_language_summary: Taking the pictures of a small circuit is now possible; turning those pictures into a reliable wiring list is the slow part. This commentary explains how hard that analysis is and how online volunteers and machine learning were being used to catch up.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution, large-extent structural maps are scarce in nervous systems because they challenge both acquisition and analysis. A dense reconstruction of the mouse inner plexiform layer—the retina’s main computational neuropil—would let new bipolar types, connectivity-based subtypes, and motion-related circuit motifs be read from anatomy.
ocar.challenge: Dense mapping of 950 neurons and their contacts requires combining crowd-sourced manual annotation with machine-learning volume segmentation on serial block-face EM, at a scale that previously blocked such maps.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, Turaga, Jain, Seung, and Denk apply crowd-sourced annotation plus ML segmentation to SBEM of the mouse inner plexiform layer (Nature 2013), densely reconstructing 950 neurons and their mutual contacts.
ocar.resolution: They characterize a new retinal bipolar interneuron type and subdivide a known type by connectivity. Emerging motifs suggest a mechanism for a known ganglion-cell response to localized motion and predict that another ganglion cell is motion sensitive.
ocar.future_work: The predicted motion-sensitive ganglion cell is an explicit experimental target; the new bipolar type invites physiological follow-up.

summaries.beginner: The layer of the mouse retina where most computing happens was reconstructed cell by cell. The map revealed a new interneuron type, split a known type by its partners, and suggested how some output cells detect motion.
summaries.intermediate: Helmstaedter et al. in Nature (2013) densely reconstruct 950 neurons and their contacts in the mouse inner plexiform layer from SBEM, combining crowd annotation and machine-learning segmentation. They report a new bipolar interneuron type and a connectivity-based split of a known type. Emerging motifs suggest a mechanism for a known local-motion ganglion-cell response and predict that another ganglion cell is motion sensitive.
summaries.advanced: 950 neurons is dense IPL in this volume, not the whole retina. Motion mechanisms are inferred from motifs plus known responses; one ganglion cell’s motion sensitivity is a prediction. DS09/DS10 mouse retina and SBF-SEM tags match.

plain_language_summary: The layer of the mouse retina where most computing happens was reconstructed cell by cell. The map revealed a new interneuron type, split a known type by its partners, and suggested how some output cells detect motion.

ocar.opportunity: Connectivity diagrams are not, by themselves, enough to understand nervous-system function. Invertebrate circuits whose connectivities are known, together with the vertebrate retina, can show what extra information—dynamics, neuromodulation, parallel circuits—is required, and how to study large circuits using lessons from small ones.
ocar.challenge: The temptation to treat a connectome as a sufficient explanation must be checked against systems where wiring is already known yet function still depends on dynamics and modulators. Parallel pathways further complicate one-to-one structure–function mapping.
ocar.action: Bargmann and Marder, in a Nature Methods (2013) Historical Perspective, ask what is needed beyond connectivity diagrams, informed by invertebrate circuits with known connectivity and by the vertebrate retina, which they argue shares neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits with those invertebrates.
ocar.resolution: They highlight dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits as general across animals, and suggest approaches to the functional organization of large circuits based on existing knowledge of small circuits.
ocar.future_work: The perspective points to studying large circuits with the same extra-connectome ingredients rather than expecting wiring diagrams alone to suffice.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring list does not by itself explain how a brain works. Drawing on small nervous systems we already understand, this essay stresses changing activity over time, chemical modulators, and parallel pathways.
summaries.intermediate: Bargmann and Marder in Nature Methods (2013) argue that connectivity diagrams are insufficient for function. Using invertebrate circuits with known wiring and the vertebrate retina, they emphasize neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits as shared features. They propose transferring small-circuit strategies to the study of large circuits.
summaries.advanced: This is a historical perspective, not new data. Catalog tags (mouse retina) reflect the retina example; the argument is comparative. No numeric results.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring list does not by itself explain how a brain works. Drawing on small nervous systems we already understand, this essay stresses changing activity over time, chemical modulators, and parallel pathways.

ocar.opportunity: Graph analysis of brain networks often uses neuroimaging without cellular resolution. The C. elegans neuronal connectome—2287 synaptic connections among 279 neurons—lets rich-club organization be tested at a cellular scale and compared with larger human neuroimaging networks.
ocar.challenge: Published interest in rich clubs needed a cellular connectome with known neuron identities, development, and behavior (locomotion) to ask whether high wiring cost is justified by adaptive value, and whether the pattern is scale-invariant.
ocar.action: Towlson, Vértes, Ahnert, Schafer, and Bullmore apply graph theory to the C. elegans neuronal connectome (Journal of Neuroscience 2013), identifying a rich club and relating it to locomotor interneurons, development, and shortest-path motifs.
ocar.resolution: They identify 11 highly connected neurons as a rich club with high efficiency and high connection distance, almost exclusively locomotor-circuit interneurons that act as connector hubs with high betweenness, many intermodular edges, and frequent occurrence on shortest paths between peripheral cells. Rich-club neurons are born early, before visible movement and before the main phase of body elongation. They conclude high wiring cost is justified by coordinated movement, recapitulating human neuroimaging and suggesting a general, scale-invariant principle.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same economical trade-off holds in other cellular connectomes is the generalization they propose.

summaries.beginner: In the worm’s wiring diagram, a small group of extra-busy cells sits at the center of many paths and is especially important for coordinated crawling. Those cells are born early, and the authors argue the extra wiring cost is worth it for movement.
summaries.intermediate: Towlson et al. in Journal of Neuroscience (2013) analyze 2287 synapses among 279 C. elegans neurons. An 11-neuron rich club—almost entirely locomotor interneurons—shows high efficiency, long connection distance, hub-like betweenness, and frequent occurrence on shortest paths between peripheral cells. Members are born before visible movement and before major body elongation. They interpret this as an economical cost–value trade-off, paralleling human neuroimaging.
summaries.advanced: 279 neurons / 2287 connections reflect the wiring diagram used; later whole-animal updates may differ. N = 11 rich-club neurons. Adaptive-value interpretation is inferential from known locomotor roles plus birth times. DS01 C. elegans matches.

plain_language_summary: In the worm’s wiring diagram, a small group of extra-busy cells sits at the center of many paths and is especially important for coordinated crawling. Those cells are born early, and the authors argue the extra wiring cost is worth it for movement.

ocar.opportunity: For Drosophila and C. elegans, image acquisition is no longer the limiting step in circuit reconstruction; extracting the circuit from large EM and optical volumes is. Software that composes deformed images, traces arbors, annotates synapses, and manages huge collections would unblock that extraction.
ocar.challenge: Image volume composition from individual deformed tiles, fast manual and semi-automatic arbor reconstruction and synapse annotation, and management of large image and annotation collections must live in one application, with export to analysis formats such as NeuroML.
ocar.action: Cardona, Saalfeld, Schindelin, Arganda-Carreras, Preibisch, Longair, Tomancak, Hartenstein, and Douglas present TrakEM2 in PLoS ONE (2012) for systematic reconstruction of neuronal circuits from large electron-microscopical and optical volumes.
ocar.resolution: TrakEM2 addresses image composition, arbor reconstruction, synapse annotation, and data management; output is a neural circuit of 3D arbors and synapses encoded in NeuroML and other formats, ready for analysis.
ocar.future_work: The tool is positioned to accelerate reconstruction now that imagery is abundant; community use on fly and worm volumes is the intended path.

summaries.beginner: Taking the pictures of fly or worm nervous systems is no longer the slow step; drawing the cells and contacts is. This free software helps stitch the pictures, trace the branches, mark the contacts, and export a wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Cardona et al. in PLoS ONE (2012) introduce TrakEM2 for reconstructing circuits from large EM and optical volumes. It handles composition of deformed images, manual and semi-automatic arbor reconstruction and synapse annotation, and management of large image and annotation collections. Output is a neural circuit of 3D arbors and synapses encoded in NeuroML and other formats, ready for analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is a software paper; speed or accuracy benchmarks are not in the abstract. Catalog tags include C. elegans and EM; the text also names Drosophila. Fiji/ImageJ ecosystem is implied by the author list but not stated in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Taking the pictures of fly or worm nervous systems is no longer the slow step; drawing the cells and contacts is. This free software helps stitch the pictures, trace the branches, mark the contacts, and export a wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: The previous decade saw a rapid increase in tools to acquire volume EM, including new SEM methods and scaled-up automated TEM. Choosing among them for reconstructing anatomical connectivity requires an explicit comparison of resolution, speed, and reliability, plus a realistic view of what wiring diagrams can and cannot explain.
ocar.challenge: Methods differ in resolution, acquisition speed, and reliability, and those tradeoffs determine whether a given circuit can be reconstructed. Wiring diagrams are likely necessary but not sufficient to understand most circuits.
ocar.action: Briggman and Bock review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012) new methods for acquiring large EM volumes, discuss tradeoffs, and assess each method’s applicability to reconstructing anatomical connectivity, including current capabilities and future prospects.
ocar.resolution: They summarize the volume-EM landscape for circuit reconstruction and argue that neuronal wiring diagrams will likely find their best application in combination with molecular biology, optogenetics, and physiology.
ocar.future_work: Combining volume EM with those complementary methods is the explicit recommended path, not EM-only explanations of circuit operation.

summaries.beginner: Several kinds of 3D electron microscopy can now photograph sizable pieces of brain. This review compares how sharp, how fast, and how reliable they are, and warns that a wiring diagram still needs other experiments to explain how a circuit works.
summaries.intermediate: Briggman and Bock in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012) review volume EM acquisition—new SEM methods and scaled automated TEM—comparing resolution, speed, and reliability for neuronal circuit reconstruction. They assess each method’s applicability to anatomical connectivity. They argue wiring diagrams are likely necessary but not sufficient, and are best combined with molecular biology, optogenetics, and physiology.
summaries.advanced: This is a review (2012 snapshot of capabilities). No new dataset. Volume EM / acquisition / graph-analysis tags match. “Necessary but not sufficient” is the conceptual caveat.

plain_language_summary: Several kinds of 3D electron microscopy can now photograph sizable pieces of brain. This review compares how sharp, how fast, and how reliable they are, and warns that a wiring diagram still needs other experiments to explain how a circuit works.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput connectomics using volume EM requires dense staining of all cells, which leads even experts to make annotation errors. Reconstruction speed, not acquisition speed, limits wiring diagrams. A faster, more reliable way to reconstruct densely labeled neurites would change that limit.
ocar.challenge: Volume labeling is slow. Redundant manual skeletons might be faster if a statistical consensus procedure can detect errors, estimate reliability, and focus reannotation on difficult locations.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk present in Nature Neuroscience (2011) manual redundant skeletonization in KNOSSOS plus RESCOP, a redundant-skeleton consensus procedure with a statistical model of how true connectivity becomes annotation decisions, including reliability estimates.
ocar.resolution: Redundant skeletonizing is about 50-fold faster than volume labeling. RESCOP detects and eliminates errors and estimates consensus-skeleton reliability. Focused reannotation of difficult locations promises a steep rise in reliability with average skeleton redundancy, aiming at nearly error-free analysis of large datasets.
ocar.future_work: The steep reliability-versus-redundancy promise is prospective; applying RESCOP to larger densely stained volumes is the intended use.

summaries.beginner: When every cell is stained, even experts make tracing mistakes. Having several people sketch the same branches and then statistically combining the sketches is reported to be much faster than coloring every voxel, with a way to estimate how trustworthy the result is.
summaries.intermediate: Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk in Nature Neuroscience (2011) introduce KNOSSOS skeletonization plus RESCOP consensus. Redundant manual skeletons are ~50× faster than volume labeling; RESCOP uses a statistical model of annotation decisions to remove errors and estimate reliability. They argue focused reannotation can raise reliability steeply with modest extra redundancy.
summaries.advanced: 50-fold is versus volume labeling, not versus later automated segmentation. “Nearly error-free” is a promised regime with focused reannotation, not a demonstrated whole-circuit error rate in the abstract. Volume EM method tag matches. Organism unspecified here.

plain_language_summary: When every cell is stained, even experts make tracing mistakes. Having several people sketch the same branches and then statistically combining the sketches is reported to be much faster than coloring every voxel, with a way to estimate how trustworthy the result is.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical local circuits involve tens of thousands of neurons each making thousands of synapses, yet wiring diagrams of their interconnections were lacking—and even a partial diagram would still need each neuron’s function. Combining in vivo physiology with network anatomy in mouse visual cortex could relate structure to function.
ocar.challenge: Two-photon calcium imaging can measure preferred orientation, but tracing a portion of those neurons’ local network requires large-scale serial-section EM. A prediction from physiology—that inhibitory interneurons receive convergent input from excitatory cells with a broad range of orientations—needed anatomical test.
ocar.action: Bock, Lee, Kerlin, Andermann, Hood, Wetzel, Yurgenson, Soucy, Kim, and Reid use two-photon calcium imaging of orientation preference in mouse V1, then large-scale serial thin-section EM to trace a portion of those neurons’ local network (Nature 2011).
ocar.resolution: Consistent with a prediction from recent physiology, inhibitory interneurons received convergent anatomical input from nearby excitatory neurons with a broad range of preferred orientations, although weak biases could not be rejected.
ocar.future_work: The combined physiology-plus-EM approach is offered as a way to study cortical structure–function; denser local-network tracing would tighten tests of weak orientation biases.

summaries.beginner: Scientists first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to lines of different tilts, then used electron microscopy to see who those cells connected to. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors of many preferred tilts, as some earlier experiments had suggested.
summaries.intermediate: Bock et al. in Nature (2011) combine in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of orientation preference in mouse primary visual cortex with large-scale serial-section EM of a portion of the local network. Inhibitory interneurons received convergent anatomical input from nearby excitatory neurons spanning a broad range of preferred orientations. Weak biases toward particular orientations could not be rejected.
summaries.advanced: The EM traces a portion of the local network, not a complete V1 connectome. Broad-range convergence is compatible with residual weak biases—the authors say those cannot be rejected. TEMCA/ssTEM and two-photon tags match. Mouse organism matches.

plain_language_summary: Scientists first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to lines of different tilts, then used electron microscopy to see who those cells connected to. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors of many preferred tilts, as some earlier experiments had suggested.

ocar.opportunity: Proper connectivity implements algorithms such as directed-motion detection in the retina, but EM connectivity analysis was limited by the scale of high-resolution data. Pairing serial block-face EM with two-photon calcium imaging could test whether starburst amacrine dendrites make direction-specific synapses onto direction-selective ganglion cells.
ocar.challenge: Technological limits had blocked large-scale high-resolution connectivity. The question is whether SAC-to-DSGC synapses depend on the ganglion cell’s preferred direction—a structural asymmetry that would constrain computational models and developmental wiring rules.
ocar.action: Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk combine SBEM with two-photon calcium imaging (Nature 2011) to map mouse starburst amacrine cell synapses onto direction-selective ganglion cells as a function of preferred direction.
ocar.resolution: SAC dendrites make highly specific synapses with DSGCs depending on the ganglion cell’s preferred direction, indicating that a structural wiring asymmetry contributes to direction selectivity. The asymmetry supports some models, rules out others, and constrains developmental synapse-formation mechanisms. The study demonstrates combining functional imaging with large-scale EM.
ocar.future_work: The same combined approach is presented as a route to other otherwise intractable circuit questions.

summaries.beginner: The retina’s motion detectors were mapped with both activity imaging and 3D electron microscopy. Star-shaped cells connect to motion-sensing output cells in a lopsided way that depends on which direction those output cells prefer, helping explain how motion is computed.
summaries.intermediate: Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk in Nature (2011) use serial block-face EM plus two-photon calcium imaging in mouse retina. Starburst amacrine dendrites synapse highly specifically onto direction-selective ganglion cells according to preferred direction. That wiring asymmetry contributes to direction selectivity, discriminates among computational models, and constrains developmental synapse-formation rules.
summaries.advanced: Asymmetry is anatomical specificity versus preferred direction measured with calcium imaging; it does not by itself quantify each model’s full computation. DS09/DS10 mouse retina, SBF-SEM, and two-photon tags match.

plain_language_summary: The retina’s motion detectors were mapped with both activity imaging and 3D electron microscopy. Star-shaped cells connect to motion-sensing output cells in a lopsided way that depends on which direction those output cells prefer, helping explain how motion is computed.

ocar.opportunity: Complete synaptic-resolution reconstructions of vertebrate circuits need new approaches. Automated serial-section TEM of rat hippocampus could test when axo-dendritic proximity predicts synapses—critical for whether coarser datasets can infer connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Peters-style predictions, touches versus synapses, and whether the largest touch marks the real synapse must be measured in densely reconstructed neuropil totaling hundreds of cubic microns.
ocar.action: Mishchenko, Hu, Špaček, Mendenhall, Harris, and Chklovskii automate ssTEM to densely reconstruct four rat hippocampal volumes totaling 670 μm³ (Neuron 2010) and quantify when proximity, touches, and largest-touch size predict synapses.
ocar.resolution: Axon density within reach of spines did not predict synaptic density along dendrites because the fraction of axons making synapses was variable—contra Peters’ rule—and a touch did not predict a synapse, yet synapse density appeared a universal fraction, 0.2, of touch density along hippocampal dendrites. The largest bouton–spine touch indicated actual synapses with about 80% precision but would miss about half of synapses. Predicting connectivity from data lacking ultrastructural synapse criteria will therefore be difficult.
ocar.future_work: The results argue that synapse-resolution ultrastructure remains necessary; coarser proximity maps are insufficient by these hippocampal metrics.

summaries.beginner: In rat hippocampus, being nearby or even touching is not the same as being connected. Mapping four tiny volumes showed that the biggest touch often is a real contact—but using only that rule would miss about half of the true connections.
summaries.intermediate: Mishchenko et al. in Neuron (2010) densely reconstruct four rat hippocampal volumes (670 μm³ total) with automated serial-section TEM. Spine-reach axon density did not predict synaptic density (variable synapsing fraction), contrary to Peters’ rule. Touches were not synapses, though synapses were ~0.2 of touches along dendrites. Largest-touch prediction reached ~80% precision but ~50% miss rate. They conclude ultrastructural synapse identification is required.
summaries.advanced: 670 μm³ across four volumes is small versus later cortical reconstructions. The 0.2 fraction is reported as appearing universal along hippocampal dendrites in this data—not proven brain-wide. 80% precision / ~half missed are largest-touch classifier stats. Organism tag “other” is rat hippocampus. ssTEM matches.

plain_language_summary: In rat hippocampus, being nearby or even touching is not the same as being connected. Mapping four tiny volumes showed that the biggest touch often is a real contact—but using only that rule would miss about half of the true connections.

ocar.opportunity: Even for C. elegans, published wiring diagrams were neither accurate nor complete and self-consistent, limiting what a cellular connectome could say about function. Assembling whole, self-consistent gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks of the hermaphrodite, then measuring topology, motifs, and linear activity patterns, could generate experimental predictions.
ocar.challenge: Materials from White et al. plus new electron micrographs must be reconciled into consistent networks. Visualization should reflect signal flow; statistics (degree, multiplicity, small-worldness) and motif modules must be tied to possible behaviors via linear systems analysis, including interaction of gap-junction and chemical networks.
ocar.action: Varshney, Chen, Paniagua, Hall, and Chklovskii assemble whole self-consistent hermaphrodite C. elegans gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks (PLoS Computational Biology 2009), propose a signal-flow visualization, compute statistical and topological properties, identify central neurons and motifs, and explore activity propagation with linear systems theory.
ocar.resolution: They report properties that help understand signal propagation, neurons that may play central processing roles, motifs as candidate modules, and activity patterns that could underlie described behaviors. Several statistics (multiplicity, motif distributions) resemble mammalian neocortex, suggesting general principles. The wiring diagram is offered to predict genetic, ablation, and stimulation experiments.
ocar.future_work: Predictions involving genetic perturbations, laser ablations, or monitoring activity after stimulation are explicitly invited.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s classic wiring list was cleaned into consistent chemical and electrical contact maps. Analyzing those maps highlights hub cells, repeating circuit scraps, and activity patterns that might explain known behaviors, and suggests new experiments.
summaries.intermediate: Varshney et al. in PLoS Computational Biology (2009) assemble self-consistent hermaphrodite C. elegans gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks from White et al. plus new EM. They visualize signal flow, compute degree, multiplicity, and small-world statistics, identify putative central neurons and motifs, and use linear systems theory for activity patterns. Multiplicity and motif distributions resemble mammalian neocortex. The diagram is meant to generate experimental predictions.
summaries.advanced: Hermaphrodite only; later male/update papers supersede completeness. Linear systems activity is a model, not recorded dynamics. Similarity to neocortex is statistical, not proof of shared computation. DS01 C. elegans / network motifs tags match.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s classic wiring list was cleaned into consistent chemical and electrical contact maps. Analyzing those maps highlights hub cells, repeating circuit scraps, and activity patterns that might explain known behaviors, and suggests new experiments.

ocar.opportunity: A gap existed between EM organelle resolution and light-microscopic tissue maps: reconstructing tissue over hundreds of micrometers with resolution to follow the thinnest processes and identify synaptic vesicles. Completely reconstructing neuronal connectivity needs such 3D EM datasets, preferably automated.
ocar.challenge: Serial-section TEM is laborious and hard to automate. Imaging an uncoated block face in an SEM risks charging; section thickness, lateral jitter, and contrast from routine TEM-style heavy-metal staining must all be solved together.
ocar.action: Denk and Horstmann demonstrate in PLoS Biology (2004) automated block-face imaging with serial sectioning inside an SEM: backscattering contrast on TEM-style stained tissue, low-vacuum (20–60 Pa H2O) to prevent charging, tracing even the thinnest axons and identifying synapses.
ocar.resolution: Stacks of several hundred sections, 50–70 nm thick, were obtained at typical lateral position jitter under 10 nm. This opens automated acquisition of EM-level 3D datasets needed to reconstruct neuronal-circuit connectivity—introducing serial block-face SEM.
ocar.future_work: The method is presented as enabling complete circuit reconstruction; applying it to identified circuits is the implied next use (later realized by the field).

summaries.beginner: Instead of collecting thousands of flimsy slices, this microscope shaves and photographs the face of a stained block, automatically, hundreds of times. The pictures are sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see connection points.
summaries.intermediate: Denk and Horstmann in PLoS Biology (2004) introduce serial block-face SEM: automated sectioning and block-face imaging in an SEM using backscattered electrons from TEM-style heavy-metal stain, with 20–60 Pa water vapor to prevent charging. They report stacks of several hundred 50–70 nm sections with typical lateral jitter under 10 nm. Resolution is sufficient to trace the thinnest axons and identify synapses.
summaries.advanced: 50–70 nm z-thickness is coarser than later isotropic FIB-SEM; jitter “typically under 10 nm” is the lateral figure. This is the method introduction, not a connectome. SBF-SEM / serial-section EM tags match. Organism unspecified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Instead of collecting thousands of flimsy slices, this microscope shaves and photographs the face of a stained block, automatically, hundreds of times. The pictures are sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see connection points.
