ocar.opportunity: Understanding a nervous system’s function requires its structure and connectivity. The nematode C. elegans, with an essentially invariant hermaphrodite nervous system of 302 neurons, offered the first animal in which those could be deduced completely from serial EM.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing from serial-section electron micrographs by hand, grouping 118 neuron classes, tracing processes in defined bundles, and cataloguing chemical synapses, neuromuscular junctions, and gap junctions for a typical animal is a monumental reconstruction problem.
ocar.action: White, Southgate, Thomson, and Brenner deduce structure and connectivity of the C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system from serial-section EM reconstructions (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 1986).
ocar.resolution: They report 302 neurons in 118 classes, simple morphologies, en passant synapses in longitudinal and circumferential bundles often beside hypodermal ridges, highly local connectivity, and muscle arms that meet motoneuron axons. Most morphologically identifiable synapses in a typical animal are described: about 5000 chemical synapses, 2000 neuromuscular junctions, and 600 gap junctions.
ocar.future_work: This wiring diagram became the foundation for decades of C. elegans circuit genetics and later updated connectomes; the abstract itself presents the completed structural catalogue.

summaries.beginner: Every nerve cell in a tiny worm—302 of them—was traced from serial electron-microscope slices, along with about 5000 chemical contacts, 2000 nerve-to-muscle contacts, and 600 electrical junctions. It is the classic complete wiring diagram of an animal’s nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: White, Southgate, Thomson, and Brenner in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (1986) reconstruct the C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system from serial EM: 302 neurons, 118 classes, simple branching, en passant synapses in stereotyped process bundles, local connectivity, and muscle arms to motoneuron axons. They describe about 5000 chemical synapses, 2000 NMJs, and 600 gap junctions in a typical animal.
summaries.advanced: Numbers are for a typical hermaphrodite reconstruction and were later revised in detail (male, updates). “Most” morphologically identifiable connections are described—not a claim of modern completeness metrics. Manual serial-section EM. DS01 C. elegans matches. This is the foundational connectome paper.

plain_language_summary: Every nerve cell in a tiny worm—302 of them—was traced from serial electron-microscope slices, along with about 5000 chemical contacts, 2000 nerve-to-muscle contacts, and 600 electrical junctions. It is the classic complete wiring diagram of an animal’s nervous system.

ocar.opportunity: Proofreading segmentation errors is the rate-limiting step in synapse-resolution connectomics. A unified, multi-species benchmark of expert-labeled split and merge decisions could train vision models to human-level proofreading and reduce labeling needed for new species and regions.
ocar.challenge: Open connectomes (mouse, human, zebrafish, fly) differ in appearance; models must handle both split correction and merge identification, stay calibrated, and degrade predictably on unseen data. Exhaustive expert labels at this scale are expensive without shared infrastructure.
ocar.action: Brown, Farkas, Razgar, and Boyden release ConnectomeBench2 on arXiv (2026): a unified dataset of over 716,485 expert-labeled proofreading decisions with more than 4,500,000 associated images spanning four major open connectomes, covering split and merge correction. They train a Vision Transformer with shared encoders for mesh geometry and EM.
ocar.resolution: A single model reaches human-level accuracy across species for split-error correction and merge-error identification, with performance scaling with data size and modality, and is well-calibrated in-distribution; distribution-distance measures predict where calibration and accuracy degrade out of distribution. Connectomics-specific pretraining and active learning show potential to cut labeling for new domains. Data and code are public (Hugging Face and GitHub).
ocar.future_work: The benchmark is offered to train and evaluate increasingly capable proofreading models; extending to new species/regions via active learning is highlighted.

summaries.beginner: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps is the slowest step. This project gathers hundreds of thousands of expert fix/don’t-fix examples from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly maps so one computer model can learn to proofread across species.
summaries.intermediate: Brown et al. on arXiv (2026) release ConnectomeBench2: >716,485 expert proofreading labels and >4,500,000 images from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly connectomes, for split and merge errors. A Vision Transformer with shared mesh and EM encoders reaches human-level accuracy across species for split correction and merge identification, scales with data and modality, and is well-calibrated in-distribution. Distance-to-training-distribution predicts out-of-distribution drops; pretraining and active learning may reduce new-domain labels.
summaries.advanced: “Human-level” is claimed for split correction and merge identification as stated—not necessarily all proofreading actions. Catalog organism tag is zebrafish; the abstract is multi-species. Dataset size numbers are from the abstract. Out-of-distribution degradation is acknowledged even with predictors of where it happens.

plain_language_summary: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps is the slowest step. This project gathers hundreds of thousands of expert fix/don’t-fix examples from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly maps so one computer model can learn to proofread across species.

ocar.opportunity: Mitochondria are integral to neuronal metabolism, and fly-brain EM volumes collected for connectomics can be reanalyzed for mitochondria as well as cells and synapses. A hemibrain-scale inventory linked to synapses and cell types would show how mitochondrial organization varies by cell type and region.
ocar.challenge: Extracting, classifying, and measuring on the order of millions of mitochondria across tens of thousands of neurons and thousands of cell types, then linking each synapse to its closest mitochondrion, is a large annotation and database problem.
ocar.action: Longden, Rivlin, Januszewski, Neace, Scheffer, Ordish, Clements, Phillips, Smith, Takemura, Umayam, Walsh, Yakal, Musial, Devine, Reiser, Plaza, and Berg extract, classify, and measure approximately 6 million mitochondria from the Drosophila Hemibrain connectome (bioRxiv; catalog year 2026), annotating location, orientation, voxel size, and appearance, linking synapses to nearest mitochondria, and extending neuPrint to store them as searchable subcellular components.
ocar.resolution: Most of the ~6 million mitochondria lie among more than 20 thousand neurons and over 5500 cell types, with volume, synapse distance, and appearance varying considerably by cell type and region. Mitochondria are larger and closer at presynapses than postsynapses (typically within one micron of a presynapse), except Kenyon cells, which have unusually small, sparse mitochondria near only about half of presynapses. Inhibitory neurons have a greater mitochondrial volume fraction than excitatory cells; dopaminergic neurons show distinct synaptic positioning; glutamatergic neurons have a high fraction of light-appearance mitochondria; and synapses with more postsynaptic partners have larger presynaptic and more distant postsynaptic mitochondria.
ocar.future_work: Public neuPrint queries of these mitochondria are the stated resource for further cell-type principles.

summaries.beginner: The same fly-brain electron-microscope volume used for wiring can also inventory the energy-producing mitochondria inside cells. Measuring millions of them shows that different cell types park differently sized mitochondria at different distances from their contacts.
summaries.intermediate: Longden et al. (bioRxiv; catalog 2026) segment ~6 million mitochondria in the Drosophila Hemibrain, spanning >20,000 neurons and >5500 cell types, and link each synapse to its nearest mitochondrion in neuPrint. They report larger, closer mitochondria at pre- versus postsynapses (typically within 1 µm of presynapses), unusual small/sparse Kenyon-cell mitochondria near only half of presynapses, higher mitochondrial volume fraction in inhibitory versus excitatory neurons, distinctive dopaminergic positioning, and more light-appearance mitochondria in glutamatergic cells. More polyadic synapses associate with larger presynaptic and more distant postsynaptic mitochondria.
summaries.advanced: Counts of about 6 million mitochondria among more than 20,000 neurons and 5,500 types are Hemibrain-specific. Appearance classes (dark/dense, light/sparse, medium) are morphological, not molecular identities, and the typical one-micron proximity applies to presynapses, with Kenyon cells as the stated exception. Catalog year 2026 versus a 2024 DOI prefix is a metadata mismatch; this card uses the shard year.

plain_language_summary: The same fly-brain electron-microscope volume used for wiring can also inventory the energy-producing mitochondria inside cells. Measuring millions of them shows that different cell types park differently sized mitochondria at different distances from their contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Valence detection in complex natural environments is critical for behaviors such as foraging, but prior Drosophila work on lateral horn and mushroom body used simple synthetic stimuli. Brain-wide connectome analysis could identify where innate and learned opponent valences converge for multimodal, real-world valence.
ocar.challenge: How the superior protocerebrum integrates LH innate and MB learned signals, including unimodal versus multimodal LH inputs and dendritic opponent organization, was unclear at whole-brain scale.
ocar.action: Wang, Yang, Liu, Gao, Lv, Zhang, Ning, and Sun use brain-wide connectome analysis (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience 2026) to identify the superior protocerebrum as integrating brain-wide multimodal inputs mainly via LH and MB and sending widespread outputs especially to the central complex, forming a convergence–divergence, autoencoder-like circuit with SP as bottleneck.
ocar.resolution: SP-input LH neurons integrate ethologically related innate valences, unimodal (for example diverse food odors) or multimodal (for example wind and temperature as bad weather), and opponent attraction/aversion plus MB learned valences update those innate signals in SP. Attractive and aversive valences, innate or learned, integrate via excitatory versus inhibitory synapses in single SP neurons, with opposite dendritic synaptic organizations for opponent valences.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest these network and dendritic structures are generalizable motifs for complex valence processing.

summaries.beginner: To decide whether something in the world is good or bad, a fruit-fly brain area collects both built-in preferences and recently learned ones, including mixtures such as food smells or bad weather. This connectome study maps that mixing station and how single cells combine opposite values.
summaries.intermediate: Wang et al. in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2026) analyze Drosophila connectome data to place the superior protocerebrum at a convergence–divergence bottleneck between LH/MB inputs and CX-biased outputs. LH neurons into SP bind ethologically related innate valences (unimodal or multimodal); MB learned valences update those innate signals. Single SP neurons integrate opponent attractive (excitatory) and aversive (inhibitory) synapses with organized dendritic compartments of opposite polarity for opponent valences.
summaries.advanced: This is connectomic circuit inference, not new physiology of SP neurons in natural scenes. Autoencoder analogy is architectural, not a trained model result. Fly organism matches; no named registry dataset in the abstract. Catalog stages empty.

plain_language_summary: To decide whether something in the world is good or bad, a fruit-fly brain area collects both built-in preferences and recently learned ones, including mixtures such as food smells or bad weather. This connectome study maps that mixing station and how single cells combine opposite values.

ocar.opportunity: Large-volume serial EM has transformed neuroscience but collecting ultrathin-section libraries (ATUM, MagC, GAUSS-EM) still constrains adoption by cost, hardware, or infrastructure. A low-cost, easily implemented wafer-based collection method would broaden access to vEM connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Newly cut sections must be cleared from the knife, confined, packed densely, and have imaging ROIs identified automatically—without expensive custom hardware—while remaining compatible with other vEM workflows.
ocar.action: Medina, Gogola, Boergens, Yang, Meirovitch, Lichtman, Kasthuri, and Wildenberg introduce DRIFT-EM in Cell Reports Methods (2026): direct retrieval by ionizer-facilitated transfer. Off-the-shelf static ionizers clear sections, a thermoplastic boundary confines them, and open-source software automates ROI identification. Modular 3D-printed components complete the platform.
ocar.resolution: DRIFT-EM achieves section packing densities comparable to established magnetic methods, with minimal setup cost and maintenance, aiming to lower barriers to creating connectomes.
ocar.future_work: Integration with other vEM workflows is explicitly facilitated by the modular open design.

summaries.beginner: Collecting thousands of ultra-thin brain slices onto wafers usually needs pricey custom gear. This design uses ordinary static ionizers, a simple boundary, and free software so more labs can gather slices for 3D electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Medina et al. in Cell Reports Methods (2026) present DRIFT-EM, a low-cost wafer-collection platform for ultrathin serial sections. Static ionizers clear sections from the knife; a thermoplastic boundary confines them; open-source software finds imaging ROIs. They report packing densities comparable to magnetic methods, with 3D-printed modular parts meant to plug into ATUM/MagC-style vEM workflows.
summaries.advanced: “Comparable” packing density is not a numeric table in the abstract. This is a collection/infrastructure method, not a released connectome. Catalog mentions ATUM + WaferMapper, MagC, serial-section EM as related methods. Organism unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Collecting thousands of ultra-thin brain slices onto wafers usually needs pricey custom gear. This design uses ordinary static ionizers, a simple boundary, and free software so more labs can gather slices for 3D electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: In most animals a small number of descending neurons connect the brain to nerve-cord circuits and motor neurons; understanding behavior requires the organization of DN-to-MN pathways. A dense Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome (companion papers) makes a first look at those networks possible at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Direct DN–MN connections may be infrequent, so communities linking descending input to walking, flight, and coordinated wing–leg control must be proofread, morphologically matched to light microscopy, and parsed at both whole-network and selected-circuit scales.
ocar.action: Cheong, Eichler, Stürner, Asinof, Champion, Marin, Oram, Sumathipala, Venkatasubramanian, Namiki, Siwanowicz, Costa, Berg, the Janelia FlyEM Project Team, Jefferis, and Card proofread and curate all DNs and MNs in the Drosophila MANC connectome (eLife 2026), match morphology to light microscopy, and analyze networks from DNs to MNs.
ocar.resolution: Direct DN–MN connections are infrequent. They identify neuron communities putatively linked to walking, flight steering and power generation, and coordinated wing and leg action. The analyses generate hypotheses for functional experiments and enable richer mechanistic study of VNC circuits.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the putative motor-system communities are explicitly invited.

summaries.beginner: Signals from a fly’s brain reach the body through a relatively small set of descending cells. Mapping those cells onto motor neurons in the male nerve cord shows that most brain commands go through intermediate partners, grouped into communities for walking, flight, and so on.
summaries.intermediate: Cheong et al. in eLife (2026) analyze the Drosophila Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome after proofreading all descending and motor neurons and matching them to light-level types. Direct DN–MN synapses are infrequent. Community structure is linked putatively to walking, flight steering/power, and coordinated wing–leg control. Companion MANC papers supply the dense VNC connectome, types, and lineages.
summaries.advanced: Community-to-behavior links are putative. Completeness depends on the companion MANC reconstruction (Takemura et al. 2024 and Marin et al. 2024 as cited). DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC) and fly tags match. This paper is organization/analysis, not the primary EM acquisition.

plain_language_summary: Signals from a fly’s brain reach the body through a relatively small set of descending cells. Mapping those cells onto motor neurons in the male nerve cord shows that most brain commands go through intermediate partners, grouped into communities for walking, flight, and so on.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons are classically polarized—dendrites in, axons out—but many have intermingled pre- and postsynaptic sites. How mixed polarity shapes connectivity across an entire nervous system was unknown. The complete adult Drosophila brain connectome (~140,000 neurons, >80 million synapses) makes a systematic map of synapse types possible.
ocar.challenge: Synapse types must be scored across compartments, cell types, and regions, including non-canonical axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, and dendro-axonic contacts, and related to a simple axis of neuronal complexity from morphology and connectivity.
ocar.action: Gross, Farah, Jana, Dorkenwald, Bock, and Deutsch systematically map synapse types in the complete adult Drosophila brain connectome (bioRxiv 2026).
ocar.resolution: Mixed polarity is widespread yet structured: about one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical, and synapse type is predictable from a neuronal-complexity axis in which low-complexity (early visual) neurons prefer dendritic interactions while larger, highly connected central neurons prefer axonal ones. Mixed polarity strongly promotes reciprocal connectivity, dominated by non-canonical motifs. Postsynaptic terminals on presynaptic boutons are a widespread motif for local reciprocal and non-canonical interactions.
ocar.future_work: These organizational principles linking architecture, synapse type, and connectivity are offered as a whole-brain framework for further functional work.

summaries.beginner: Not every brain contact is the textbook pattern of an outgoing cable onto an incoming branch. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this study finds mixed sending and receiving cells are common but orderly: simple visual cells tend to talk via dendrites, complex central cells via axons, and mixed cells often talk back and forth.
summaries.intermediate: Gross et al. on bioRxiv (2026) survey synapse types across an adult Drosophila whole-brain connectome (~140,000 neurons, >80 million synapses). Mixed polarity is widespread and structured; ~one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical (axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, dendro-axonic). A morphology/connectivity complexity axis predicts synapse type. Mixed polarity promotes reciprocity via non-canonical motifs, including postsynaptic terminals on boutons.
summaries.advanced: ~140,000 neurons and >80 million synapses are the abstract’s whole-brain figures. The one-third non-canonical fraction applies to synapses between polarized neurons. Complexity-axis “prediction” is a reported relationship, not an independent test set in the abstract. Fly / graph analysis tags match; no registry dataset named.

plain_language_summary: Not every brain contact is the textbook pattern of an outgoing cable onto an incoming branch. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this study finds mixed sending and receiving cells are common but orderly: simple visual cells tend to talk via dendrites, complex central cells via axons, and mixed cells often talk back and forth.

ocar.opportunity: The insect neck connective is a physical and information bottleneck between brain and ventral nerve cord, carrying descending, ascending, and sensory ascending neurons essential for sensorimotor control. Integrating three EM datasets could yield a complete female DN/AN connectome and comparison with male nerve cord, including sexually dimorphic circuits.
ocar.challenge: Neurons must be proofread, matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes, and aligned to light-level driver lines. Completeness across the neck for an adult animal had not been achieved.
ocar.action: Stürner, Brooks, Serratosa Capdevila, Morris, Javier, Fang, Gkantia, Cachero, Beckett, Marin, Schlegel, Champion, Moitra, Richards, Klemm, Kugel, Namiki, Cheong, Kovalyak, Tenshaw, Parekh, Phelps, Mark, Dorkenwald, Bates, Matsliah, Yu, McKellar, Sterling, Seung, Murthy, Tuthill, Lee, Card, Costa, Jefferis, and Eichler integrate three EM datasets (Nature 2025) for a complete connectomic description of Drosophila female ANs and DNs compared with male nerve cord, matching 51% of DN cell types to light-level driver lines and classifying all ascending populations.
ocar.resolution: They describe connected DN–AN chains spanning the neck that may subserve motor sequences, and complete sexually dimorphic DN/AN populations, with detailed circuits for male courtship (DNa12/aSP22), song production (AN neurons from hemilineage 08B), and female ovipositor extrusion (DNp13). The work provides EM-level circuit analyses spanning the entire adult CNS.
ocar.future_work: Matched driver lines for 51% of DN types enable functional tests; remaining unmatched types are an annotation gap.

summaries.beginner: The bundle between a fly’s head and body was mapped by combining three electron-microscope datasets, including comparison of females and males. The map covers brain-to-body command cells, body-to-brain reporters, and sex-specific circuits for courtship, song, and egg laying.
summaries.intermediate: Stürner et al. in Nature (2025) integrate three EM volumes for a complete female Drosophila descending/ascending neuron connectome versus the male nerve cord, matching neurons across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes. 51% of DN types match light-level driver lines; all ascending populations are classified. Findings include DN–AN chains across the neck and dimorphic circuits (DNa12/aSP22 courtship, 08B ANs for song, DNp13 ovipositor extrusion).
summaries.advanced: Completeness is for AN/DN populations of the neck connective as reconstructed across three datasets, not every VNC intrinsic. 51% DN-to-driver match leaves nearly half without named lines in this paper. Motor-sequence role of DN–AN chains is suggested (“may subserve”). DS07 VNC / fly / EM tags match.

plain_language_summary: The bundle between a fly’s head and body was mapped by combining three electron-microscope datasets, including comparison of females and males. The map covers brain-to-body command cells, body-to-brain reporters, and sex-specific circuits for courtship, song, and egg laying.

ocar.opportunity: Visual regions often occupy about half the brain, with neurons organized on spatial maps whose shapes relate to visual roles. A connectome of the right optic lobe of a male Drosophila, plus genetic drivers matched to types, would let anatomy, neurotransmitters, and connectivity jointly define a complete visual-neuron inventory.
ocar.challenge: Classifying on the order of 53,000 neurons into hundreds of types requires a computational framework to quantify anatomy, integrated with connectivity, transmitter identity, and expert curation, plus reagents for targeted experiments.
ocar.action: Nern, Loesche, Takemura, Burnett, Dreher, Gruntman, Hoeller, Huang, Januszewski, Klapoetke, Koskela, Longden, Lu, Preibisch, Qiu, Rogers, Seenivasan, Zhao, Bogovic, and many Janelia/FlyEM colleagues present a FIB-SEM connectome of the right optic lobe of a male D. melanogaster (Nature 2025), with a quantitative anatomical framework, classification, systematic descriptions, and split-GAL4 lines matched to the catalogue.
ocar.resolution: About 53,000 neurons are classified into 732 types, about half newly named, establishing a basis for relating visual-neuron shape to spatial vision. An extensive split-GAL4 collection is matched to the neuron-type catalogue, unlocking systematic visual-system experiments.
ocar.future_work: The inventory and driver lines are offered as a foundation for deeper sensory-processing studies in Drosophila.

summaries.beginner: Half a fly’s brain is devoted to seeing. This project maps the right visual lobe of a male fly, sorts about 53,000 cells into 732 types—many newly named—and pairs those types with genetic tools so experiments can target them.
summaries.intermediate: Nern et al. in Nature (2025) report a FIB-SEM connectome of the right optic lobe of a male Drosophila, classifying about 53,000 neurons into 732 types, about half newly named, using quantified anatomy plus connectivity, neurotransmitter identity, and expert curation. They share split-GAL4 lines matched to the catalogue. The resource is offered as a basis for relating cell shape to spatial vision.
summaries.advanced: ~53,000 neurons / 732 types / ~half newly named are the abstract’s figures. This is the right optic lobe of one male, not both lobes or the central brain. Split-GAL4 coverage relative to all 732 types is described as extensive, not necessarily complete. FIB-SEM / fly tags match. Acquisition/infrastructure stages match.

plain_language_summary: Half a fly’s brain is devoted to seeing. This project maps the right visual lobe of a male fly, sorts about 53,000 cells into 732 types—many newly named—and pairs those types with genetic tools so experiments can target them.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping neurons and synapses at nanoscale with dense labeling is required to relate wiring to molecular identity. Light microscopy can visualize specific molecules, but dense synapse-level circuit reconstruction by light had been out of reach because of limits in resolution, contrast, and volumetric imaging. A hydrogel-expansion method that reaches synapse-level reconstructions while keeping molecular information would enable readily adopted phenotyping.
ocar.challenge: Expansion, dense labeling, and comprehensive deep-learning segmentation must work together so connectivity and molecules occupy the same volume reconstruction of mammalian brain tissue.
ocar.action: Tavakoli, Lyudchik, Januszewski, Vistunou, Agudelo Dueñas, Vorlaufer, Sommer, Kreuzinger, Oliveira, Cenameri, Novarino, Jain, and Danzl describe LICONN in Nature (2025): light-microscopy-based connectomics integrating engineered hydrogel embedding and expansion with deep-learning segmentation and connectivity analysis, incorporating molecular information into synapse-level reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: LICONN is presented as allowing synapse-level mapping of brain tissue with simultaneous molecular measurement, enabling quantification of cellular properties and multimodal analysis, and synapse-level phenotyping in biological experiments in a readily adoptable manner.
ocar.future_work: Adoption for biological phenotyping experiments is the stated purpose; independent comparisons to EM connectomes are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can map every contact but not easily the molecules in those cells. This light-microscope method swells the tissue and uses computer tracing so wiring and molecular stains can be read together at the scale of individual contacts.
summaries.intermediate: Tavakoli et al. in Nature (2025) introduce LICONN: hydrogel expansion plus engineered embedding, dense labeling, and deep-learning segmentation to reconstruct mammalian brain tissue at synapse level while retaining molecular information. They present it as enabling synapse-level phenotyping and multimodal analysis. The workflow is positioned as more readily adoptable than EM-only connectomics.
summaries.advanced: “Synapse-level” is the authors’ claim for this LM method; EM remains the classical gold standard and is not numerically compared here. Organism/dataset tags are empty; tissue is mammalian brain as stated. Readily adoptable is a positioning claim, not a user-study result in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can map every contact but not easily the molecules in those cells. This light-microscope method swells the tissue and uses computer tracing so wiring and molecular stains can be read together at the scale of individual contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Context-appropriate behavior depends on integrated action across the brain, but how activity is coordinated across regions and how structure enables those interactions remain open. Technical advances now make brain-wide maps of structure and function—activity maps, connectomes, cell atlases—feasible in C. elegans and Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: Global maps must still capture complexities known from specific networks if they are to yield accurate models of whole-brain function. Integrating activity, connectivity, and cell-type atlases is a conceptual as well as technical problem.
ocar.action: Kramer and Flavell review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2024) progress in building and integrating brain-wide maps in invertebrates, focusing on C. elegans and D. melanogaster, where global maps have recently been produced, and they describe circuit motifs from specific networks that models must capture.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys recent global maps of these nervous systems and highlights motifs from focused studies as the complexities that whole-brain models must include.
ocar.future_work: Accurate whole-brain models will need to incorporate those motifs, not only coarse regional maps.

summaries.beginner: For tiny animals we can now map the whole nervous system’s wiring, cell types, and activity. This review asks how to put those maps together, using worm and fly examples, and warns that small circuit tricks still have to be in the big models.
summaries.intermediate: Kramer and Flavell in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2024) review brain-wide structural and functional maps in C. elegans and Drosophila, including activity maps, connectomes, and cell atlases. They also describe circuit motifs from specific networks that whole-brain models must capture. Coordination of activity across regions remains an open question the maps are meant to address.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not new data. Catalog DS01 / elegans tags undersell the fly half of the article; the abstract names both species. Motifs are pointed to, not enumerated, in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: For tiny animals we can now map the whole nervous system’s wiring, cell types, and activity. This review asks how to put those maps together, using worm and fly examples, and warns that small circuit tricks still have to be in the big models.

ocar.opportunity: EM and X-ray micro/holographic-nano tomography connectomics datasets are growing across species, regions, and techniques, often past petascale, each with unique metadata. Standardization would enable comparative connectomics and interoperability, as other neuroimaging modalities already have community standards.
ocar.challenge: EM and XRM/XHN connectomics lacked adopted image and experimental metadata standards, isolating datasets and blocking integration. A working group of stakeholders was needed to draft versioned standards supporting metadata services and software.
ocar.action: Wimbish, Guittari, Rose, Rivera, Rivlin, Hinton, Matelsky, Stock, Wester, Johnson, and Gray-Roncal report version 1.1 Image and Experimental Metadata Standards for EM and XRM/XHN (arXiv 2024), developed by a community working group, with annotation standards in a companion document and definitions on a community GitHub.
ocar.resolution: The standards aim to support metadata services and future software, enable comparative analysis, improve interoperability between connectomics tools, and continue to be refined by the neuroinformatics community.
ocar.future_work: Community refinement and implementation in metadata services and software are explicitly hoped for; annotation standards live in a companion document.

summaries.beginner: Giant electron-microscope and X-ray brain datasets each come with their own messy labels, making them hard to compare. This paper proposes a shared checklist for how those pictures and experiments should be described so software and scientists can talk to each other.
summaries.intermediate: Wimbish et al. on arXiv (2024) present version 1.1 community metadata standards for EM and X-ray micro/holographic-nano tomography connectomics imaging and experiments. A stakeholder working group drafted them to match standards already common in other neuroimaging. Companion annotation standards and a GitHub definition set accompany the document. Goals include comparative connectomics and tool interoperability.
summaries.advanced: This is a standards document, not a biological result. Adoption is prospective. uuid equals work_id (no DOI in catalog). Proofreading/graph-analysis tags are loosely related; the paper is infrastructure/metadata. Organism unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Giant electron-microscope and X-ray brain datasets each come with their own messy labels, making them hard to compare. This paper proposes a shared checklist for how those pictures and experiments should be described so software and scientists can talk to each other.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM connectomes allow nanoscale quantification of cell-biological features underpinning circuits, producing multidimensional datasets that benefit from dimensionality reduction and graphs of neuronal relationships. An open platform linking those abstractions back to the underlying features would let researchers compare connectomes across development.
ocar.challenge: High-level graph analytics are often disconnected from the cell biology in the volume. Comparing published C. elegans brain neuropils across stages requires an intuitive interface that spans both.
ocar.action: Koonce, Emerson, Bhaskar, Kuchroo, Moyle, Arroyo-Morales, Vázquez Martínez, Emerson, Krishnaswamy, Mohler, and Colón-Ramos present NeuroSC/NeuroSCAN (bioRxiv 2024), an open-source online platform bridging graph analytics with cell-biological features, demonstrated on a series of published C. elegans brain neuropils.
ocar.resolution: Integrated representations facilitate comparisons across connectomes and catalyze insights into structure–function relationships and developmental change. The platform is designed for intuitive examination from high-level neuronal-relationship abstractions down to the cell-biological features that underpin them.
ocar.future_work: The tool is aimed at further cross-connectome comparisons in C. elegans and, by design, other vEM neuropils.

summaries.beginner: Connectome pictures contain not just who talks to whom but the tiny cell parts that make those talks possible. This website helps compare worm brain maps across ages by linking big-picture relationship graphs back to those parts.
summaries.intermediate: Koonce et al. on bioRxiv (2024) introduce NeuroSC (NeuroSCAN), an open-source platform combining data-science graph analytics of neuronal relationships with cell-biological features in volume EM. Using published C. elegans brain neuropils, they show integrated views that compare connectomes. The views are meant to reveal structure–function and developmental changes from high-level abstractions down to nanoscale features.
summaries.advanced: Insights are demonstrated on published C. elegans neuropils, not a new EM volume. “Catalyzing new insights” is the authors’ framing. DS01 / elegans / volume EM / infrastructure tags match.

plain_language_summary: Connectome pictures contain not just who talks to whom but the tiny cell parts that make those talks possible. This website helps compare worm brain maps across ages by linking big-picture relationship graphs back to those parts.

ocar.opportunity: How the body interacts with the brain for vital functions such as feeding is fundamental. A whole-animal scanning TEM volume of Drosophila can map the entire enteric nervous system’s synaptic links to the brain via the insect vagus, revealing a gut–brain loop for swallowing.
ocar.challenge: Piezo mechanosensors in the esophagus, serotonergic brain neurons, food-value information, and swallowing motor neurons must be placed in one synaptic-resolution loop, including an unexpected axo-axonic motor-to-mechanosensory contact.
ocar.action: Schoofs, Miroschnikow, Schlegel, Zinke, Schneider-Mizell, Cardona, and Pankratz map neuronal circuits connecting the entire enteric nervous system to the brain via the insect vagus in a whole-animal Drosophila STEM volume (Current Biology 2024).
ocar.resolution: They identify a feedback loop: esophageal Piezo mechanosensors report food passage to six serotonergic brain neurons that, with food-value information, enhance serotonin-receptor-7 motor neurons driving swallowing. Glutamatergic esophageal motor axons make axo-axonic synapses onto the mechanosensors that signal to the serotonergic cells. Ongoing motor activity is thus strengthened by serotonin upon completing a biologically meaningful action—an elemental architecture that may represent an ancient form of motor learning.
ocar.future_work: The evolutionary “ancient motor learning” framing is interpretive; functional tests of the six serotonergic cells and 5-HT7 motoneurons are implied by the circuit.

summaries.beginner: A complete fly-body electron-microscope map shows how swallowing is tuned. Sensors in the food tube tell six serotonin cells in the brain that food is moving, and those cells then boost the motor cells that swallow, strengthening a successful action.
summaries.intermediate: Schoofs et al. in Current Biology (2024) reconstruct gut–brain circuits in a whole-animal Drosophila STEM volume, including the insect vagus. Piezo esophageal mechanosensors innervate six brain serotonergic neurons that, together with food-value cues, enhance 5-HT7-expressing swallowing motoneurons. Motoneuron axons also synapse onto the mechanosensors. They interpret this as serotonergic strengthening of motor activity after a meaningful action.
summaries.advanced: “Entire enteric nervous system” is the authors’ completeness claim for this volume. Six serotonergic neurons is a specific count. Ancient-motor-learning language is a hypothesis. TEM/STEM method and fly tags match. Acquisition stage matches imaging of the volume.

plain_language_summary: A complete fly-body electron-microscope map shows how swallowing is tuned. Sensors in the food tube tell six serotonin cells in the brain that food is moving, and those cells then boost the motor cells that swallow, strengthening a successful action.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic volumes now reach tera- to petascale with diverse appearance from different preparations, while labeled synapses are often smaller than 0.001% of the volume. Domain-adaptive synapse detection—using in-domain labels to generalize to unlabeled out-of-domain data—is urgently needed, but few natural-image domain-adaptation methods have been benchmarked on connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Biologically diverse Megaphragma viggianii brain regions from three whole-brain datasets differ in appearance. A public challenge must provide 3D pre- and postsynapse coordinates plus one-to-many connectivity, baselines, and evaluation, and remain available after the meeting.
ocar.action: Li, Li, Chen, Huang, Zou, Xiao, Shinomiya, Gunn, Gupta, Polilov, Xu, Zhang, Xiong, Pfister, Wei, and Wu annotated 14 volumes from diverse M. viggianii brain regions across three whole-brain datasets and organized the WASPSYN challenge at ISBI 2023 (IEEE TMI 2024), with tasks, a proposed baseline, evaluation, and discussion of limits and neuroscience impact.
ocar.resolution: The challenge (and ongoing CodaLab competition) supplies a domain-adaptation benchmark for synapse detection with pre/post coordinates and connectivity. Successful algorithms may potentially revolutionize real-world connectomics research, per the authors.
ocar.future_work: The competition remains open for new methods; limitations of the challenge are discussed in the paper.

summaries.beginner: Computers trained to find connections in one insect-brain dataset often fail on the next because the pictures look different. This contest released 14 labeled micro-wasp brain volumes so methods can be tested on that jump between datasets.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2024) describe WASPSYN (ISBI 2023): 14 annotated Megaphragma viggianii volumes from three whole-brain datasets, with 3D pre- and postsynaptic coordinates and one-to-many connectivity, plus a baseline and evaluation protocol for domain-adaptive synapse detection. Labeled training data are framed as often <0.001% of application volumes. The challenge remains at the stated CodaLab URL.
summaries.advanced: Impact language (“may potentially revolutionize”) is promotional. Challenge limitations are acknowledged but not enumerated in the abstract. Organism is a micro-wasp, not Drosophila. Preparation/proofreading/synapses tags match the task. No numeric winner scores in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Computers trained to find connections in one insect-brain dataset often fail on the next because the pictures look different. This contest released 14 labeled micro-wasp brain volumes so methods can be tested on that jump between datasets.

ocar.opportunity: Most neuroscience model organisms lack high-resolution maps of complex visual circuitry. The microinsect Megaphragma viggianii, small yet behaviorally non-trivial, offers tractable whole-organism connectomics. Reconstructing its compound eye and lamina would define a minimal flying-insect visual front end versus fly and honeybee.
ocar.challenge: Whole-head serial EM must support optical analysis of ommatidia and a synaptic connectome of the first visual neuropil, including stereotyped versus specialized ommatidia, with only 29 ommatidia per eye and a handful of lamina types.
ocar.action: Chua, Gunn, Makarova, Hess, Polilov, Chklovskii, Villani, Cohen, Thasin, Wu, Shefter, Pang, and Xu image the whole Megaphragma head with serial EM (Current Biology 2023), reconstruct the compound eye, analyze ommatidial optics, and reconstruct the lamina connectome.
ocar.resolution: Compared with fruit fly and honeybee, the visual system is highly simplified: 29 ommatidia per eye and 6 lamina neuron types. Features are both stereotypical among most ommatidia and specialized in some. The authors argue these “barebones” circuits are critical for flying insects and will facilitate computational models of insect visual processing.
ocar.future_work: Computational models using this minimal visual front end are explicitly invited.

summaries.beginner: A tiny wasp-like insect with only 29 facets per eye had its whole head photographed and its first visual station wired out. The simplified circuit, compared with flies and bees, is offered as the essential core of insect vision for flying.
summaries.intermediate: Chua et al. in Current Biology (2023) reconstruct the early visual system of adult Megaphragma viggianii from whole-head serial EM: 29 ommatidia per eye, optical properties of those ommatidia, and a lamina connectome with 6 neuron types, highly simplified versus fruit fly and honeybee. They report both stereotyped and specialized ommatidial features. The circuit is presented as a barebones flying-insect visual system for modeling.
summaries.advanced: 29 ommatidia / 6 lamina types are the headline simplifications. Catalog organism tag is fly; the species is a microinsect, not Drosophila—this card follows the abstract. Modeling stage tag matches the stated use. Completeness is early visual system (eye + lamina), not whole brain.

plain_language_summary: A tiny wasp-like insect with only 29 facets per eye had its whole head photographed and its first visual station wired out. The simplified circuit, compared with flies and bees, is offered as the essential core of insect vision for flying.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale neuronal EM segmentations require automated, scalable error detection. Errors at neurite tips are especially damaging because they usually mean many synapses are split from the parent neuron. A mesh-based method that flags tip errors and suggests continuations could accelerate proofreading.
ocar.challenge: Manual proofreading is laborious and still necessary. Detecting which tips are erroneous and guiding readers to likely continuations, then measuring correction rate in a semi-automated pipeline, is the engineering challenge.
ocar.action: Joyce, Chalavadi, Chan, Tanna, Xenes, Kuo, Rose, Matelsky, Kitchell, Bishop, Rivlin, Villafañe-Delgado, and Wester propose a mesh-processing pipeline that identifies potential error locations near neuronal tips and implement it in a semi-automated proofreading workflow (bioRxiv 2023).
ocar.resolution: The approach systematically highlights likely inaccurate areas and guides proofreaders toward potential continuations, accelerating error correction in an implemented pipeline. Tip-error detection is emphasized as protecting synaptic completeness of reconstructions.
ocar.future_work: Broader deployment on additional EM volumes is implied by the scalability motivation.

summaries.beginner: When a computer tracing of a neuron stops too soon, many contacts are left off that cell. This method looks at the 3D mesh near those dead ends to guess which ones are mistakes and where the branch probably continues, so human checkers can work faster.
summaries.intermediate: Joyce et al. on bioRxiv (2023) introduce a mesh-based detector of likely segmentation errors near neuronal tips, a high-impact error class that falsely splits synapses from parent neurons. Integrated into a semi-automated proofreading pipeline, it highlights probable error sites and candidate continuations. The authors report that this guidance accelerates correction versus unguided manual proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Acceleration is claimed without a numeric factor in the abstract. No organism or dataset is named. Mesh methods assume a segmentation mesh exists. Semi-automated, not fully automatic, proofreading. Segmentation/proofreading/infrastructure tags match.

plain_language_summary: When a computer tracing of a neuron stops too soon, many contacts are left off that cell. This method looks at the 3D mesh near those dead ends to guess which ones are mistakes and where the branch probably continues, so human checkers can work faster.

ocar.opportunity: EM wiring diagrams invite cross-species comparison: C. elegans has been framed as an approximately feedforward sensorimotor circuit with overrepresented three-cell feedforward-loop motifs, while a larval zebrafish brainstem oculomotor module offers a vertebrate contrast at cellular precision.
ocar.challenge: Whether cyclic three-cell motifs appear in any EM connectome was open; vertebrate sequence/integrator models of the oculomotor system specifically predict recurrence. Aligning cellular cycles with stochastic-block-model group cycles, and noting recurrence to the same neuron, requires a reconstructed oculomotor module.
ocar.action: Yang, Vishwanathan, Wu, Kemnitz, Ih, Turner, Lee, Tartavull, Silversmith, Jordan, David, Bland, Sterling, Goldman, Aksay, and Seung analyze three-cell motifs in a larval zebrafish brainstem oculomotor wiring diagram (Current Biology 2023), contrasting C. elegans feedforwardness, and fit a stochastic block model of neuronal groups.
ocar.resolution: The three-cycle is highly overrepresented in the zebrafish oculomotor module—a first for EM wiring diagrams in invertebrates or mammals as cited. Cellular three-cycles align with a three-cycle of groups in a stochastic block model, yet show more specificity than group cycles explain; recurrence to the same neuron is surprisingly common. Cyclic structure coexists with the classic vestibulo-ocular reflex arc and could matter for recurrent integrator models of oculomotor temporal integration.
ocar.future_work: The cyclic motif is offered as relevant to recurrent theories of oculomotor function; causal tests are outside this anatomy paper.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring is often drawn as a one-way chain from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish’s eye-movement circuit, three-cell loops are unusually common, including loops that return to the same cell—more like a recycling loop than a one-way conveyor.
summaries.intermediate: Yang et al. in Current Biology (2023) compare motif structure in a larval zebrafish brainstem oculomotor connectome with the C. elegans feedforward picture. Three-cycles are highly overrepresented, unlike prior EM diagrams cited. Cycles align with a three-group stochastic block model but are more specific, with frequent recurrence to the same neuron, coexisting with the horizontal VOR arc and potentially supporting recurrent integrator models.
summaries.advanced: “First for any neuronal wiring diagram reconstructed by EM” is the authors’ claim relative to cited invertebrate and mammalian maps. Overrepresentation is for this oculomotor module, not the whole zebrafish brain. Catalog datasets DS01 and DS15 reflect the comparison; the new anatomy is zebrafish. Function of cycles is hypothetical.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring is often drawn as a one-way chain from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish’s eye-movement circuit, three-cell loops are unusually common, including loops that return to the same cell—more like a recycling loop than a one-way conveyor.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes now regularly yield large neuron–synapse graphs, but they are mostly one-of-a-kind, so discovering unhypothesized interesting subgraphs is statistically and computationally hard. A method that finds significant directed or undirected motifs from a single graph, with proper randomization, would address a core unsolved problem in biological motif discovery.
ocar.challenge: Exhaustive subgraph search is intractable; standard random-graph nulls mislead significance; small sample sizes of host graphs prevent easy replication. Progressive refinement and better randomization are needed, with a usable software package.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Robinette, Wester, Gray-Roncal, Johnson, and Reilly present a motif-discovery approach (bioRxiv 2023) that derives statistically significant undirected or directed motifs from a single graph, with improved randomization, a progressive-refinement search, sampling correction, and an open-source Python package, demonstrated on C. elegans and the Drosophila ellipsoid body.
ocar.resolution: They show common pitfalls in motif significance testing, that improved randomization and sampling correction enable significance testing of target motifs, and that standard random-graph models can mislead. Preliminary real-world results are reported on the C. elegans connectome and Drosophila ellipsoid body, and code is released as a Python package.
ocar.future_work: The package is intended for further biological graphs; the abstract frames results on fly ellipsoid body and worm as preliminary.

summaries.beginner: Looking for repeating little wiring patterns in a unique brain map is hard: there is usually only one map, and checking every pattern is impossible. This method hunts for patterns that show up more than they should by chance, using a fairer shuffle of the same map, and is tested on worm and fly data.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. on bioRxiv (2023) propose single-graph motif discovery for directed or undirected subgraphs with occurrence counts tested against improved randomized graphs, plus progressive refinement to control cost and sampling correction. They warn that standard random-graph nulls mislead. Demonstrations include the C. elegans connectome and Drosophila ellipsoid body; an open-source Python package is provided.
summaries.advanced: Fly results are ellipsoid body, not whole-brain. “Preliminary” is the authors’ word for real-world demos. Statistical significance depends on the randomization scheme they critique/improve. DS01 elegans tag matches; fly ellipsoid body is additional. Acquisition tag is weakly related; this is graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Looking for repeating little wiring patterns in a unique brain map is hard: there is usually only one map, and checking every pattern is impossible. This method hunts for patterns that show up more than they should by chance, using a fairer shuffle of the same map, and is tested on worm and fly data.

ocar.opportunity: Fully automated instance segmentation of EM connectomics still fails on some volumes, so manual reconstruction remains necessary—but even careful manuals leave numerous small errors. Learning to correct “sloppy” annotations could cut annotation time while reaching near ground-truth morphology, including on datasets current automatic methods cannot segment at scale.
ocar.challenge: Marker-based 2D instance segmentation and region growing must handle sloppy object outlines by shrinking and expanding them. The method should work on public benchmarks and on large-scale problems such as a new octopus dataset that existing algorithms cannot automatically segment at scale.
ocar.action: Chen, Bangalore Renuka, Mi, Lichtman, Shavit, and Meirovitch design a marker-based 2D instance-segmentation/region-growing method (CVPR Workshops 2023) that learns to correct sloppy manual annotations by reducing and expanding them, reporting a new state of the art among region-growing algorithms on challenging EM stacks.
ocar.resolution: Correction yields high-quality morphological reconstructions (near ground truth) while cutting annotation time about 8× on several connectomics examples. They demonstrate accuracy on public benchmarks and large-scale neuron reconstructions, including a new octopus dataset not automatically segmentable at scale by existing algorithms.
ocar.future_work: Applying the corrector to other hard EM volumes where automation fails is the implied use, especially the octopus case.

summaries.beginner: People tracing cells in electron-microscope pictures often draw slightly messy outlines. A computer that learns to tidy those outlines can get near-expert shapes about eight times faster, including on an octopus dataset that automatic methods cannot yet handle at scale.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. at CVPR Workshops (2023) learn to correct sloppy EM annotations via a marker-based 2D instance-segmentation and region-growing algorithm, claiming state-of-the-art among region-growing methods on challenging EM stacks. They report near-ground-truth morphology with about 8× faster annotation on several connectomics examples. Demonstrations include public benchmarks and a new octopus volume that existing automatic segmenters cannot do at scale.
summaries.advanced: ~8× is for several examples, not a universal constant. SOTA is among region-growing algorithms as stated. Octopus dataset (DS21) is highlighted as automation-hard. 2D marker-based correction is not full 3D agglomeration. Catalog organism “other” matches octopus.

plain_language_summary: People tracing cells in electron-microscope pictures often draw slightly messy outlines. A computer that learns to tidy those outlines can get near-expert shapes about eight times faster, including on an octopus dataset that automatic methods cannot yet handle at scale.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila uniquely combines complex behavior, genetics, dense CNS connectomes, and growing transcriptomes, but researchers struggle to find, access, integrate, and reuse (FAIR) the relevant images, types, and reagents. A single atlas application covering larva and adult whole CNS could support hypothesis generation and experiment design.
ocar.challenge: Massive, heterogeneous data—3D neurons and regions, connectomics, transcriptomics, reagent expression—must be searchable by name, location, connectivity, type, or properties, with linked 2D/3D browsers and literature-curated descriptions, under open licenses.
ocar.action: Court, Costa, Pilgrim, Millburn, Holmes, McLachlan, Larkin, Matentzoglu, Kir, Parkinson, Brown, O’Kane, Armstrong, Jefferis, and Osumi-Sutherland present Virtual Fly Brain (Frontiers in Physiology 2023): a web application and API integrating those data for larval and adult CNS using FAIR principles.
ocar.resolution: Users can search by text, clicking 3D images, search-by-image, type (for example dopaminergic neuron), or properties (for example synaptic input in the antennal lobe), and results include cross-registered 3D images that can be browsed or downloaded plus curated cell-type and region descriptions. Solutions are described as potentially extensible to vertebrate atlasing.
ocar.future_work: Extending the same FAIR atlasing pattern to vertebrates is explicitly suggested.

summaries.beginner: Fly researchers have more maps, gene tools, and cell lists than anyone can keep in their head. Virtual Fly Brain is a website that lets you search that pile by name, location, or connections and see the matching 3D cells.
summaries.intermediate: Court et al. in Frontiers in Physiology (2023) describe Virtual Fly Brain (virtualflybrain.org): a FAIR web app and API integrating 3D neuron and region images, connectomics, transcriptomics, and reagent expression for Drosophila larval and adult whole CNS. Search includes text, 3D clicks, image query, and type or property queries. Returns include cross-registered imagery and literature-curated descriptions.
summaries.advanced: This is an infrastructure/atlas paper, not a new connectome. Extensibility to vertebrates is potential. Coverage “whole CNS” is the resource claim. Fly / infrastructure tags match. No numeric performance metrics in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fly researchers have more maps, gene tools, and cell lists than anyone can keep in their head. Virtual Fly Brain is a website that lets you search that pile by name, location, or connections and see the matching 3D cells.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes are graphs that may have colored edges (e.g. excitatory versus inhibitory). Most analyses look for hypothesized motifs, but a goal of connectomics is unhypothesized, biologically significant subgraphs—requiring large-scale enumeration of all unique motifs, including edge types.
ocar.challenge: Exact subgraph enumeration is computationally expensive on edge-dense wiring diagrams; most methods ignore edge types, which can change motif function. Parallel, community-based, type-aware enumeration on many connectomes is required at trillion-subgraph scale.
ocar.action: Matejek, Wei, Chen, Tsourakakis, Mitzenmacher, and Pfister propose a parallel general-purpose subgraph enumeration strategy, a divide-and-conquer community-based enumeration per brain region, and edge-type differentiation (Scientific Reports 2022), demonstrating on eleven connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They publish overviews of 26 trillion enumerated subgraphs that required approximately 9.25 years of computation time, for future analyses, with colored directed subgraph counts that reflect biological edge labels.
ocar.future_work: The published overviews are intended for future biological interpretation of unhypothesized motifs.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams can be treated as colored maps of who talks to whom and whether the talk is go or stop. This computing project listed enormous numbers of small repeating patterns across eleven such maps so scientists can find motifs they did not already expect.
summaries.intermediate: Matejek et al. in Scientific Reports (2022) present parallel, community-partitioned enumeration of edge-colored directed subgraphs on connectomes, distinguishing edge types that can change motif function. On eleven connectomes they enumerate 26 trillion subgraphs, requiring about 9.25 years of compute. They release overviews for later analysis, aiming at unhypothesized biologically significant motifs rather than only hypothesized ones.
summaries.advanced: 26 trillion subgraphs and ~9.25 years compute are the scale figures; they are not a biological result. Eleven unnamed connectomes in the abstract. Enumeration is exact as framed, with cost as the caveat. Network-motifs method tag matches. Organism unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams can be treated as colored maps of who talks to whom and whether the talk is go or stop. This computing project listed enormous numbers of small repeating patterns across eleven such maps so scientists can find motifs they did not already expect.

ocar.opportunity: Neural circuitry structure shapes function, but studies usually trade coarse large-scale organization against fine cell-type wiring. A synapse-resolution adult female Drosophila hemibrain (>20,000 neurons, 10 million synapses) lets community detection resolve modules from thousands of neurons down to tens, testing hierarchy and recovering known pathways plus finer structure.
ocar.challenge: Analyzing a network of this size needs efficient community detection. Maximizing a generalized modularity density measure and resolving communities across scales must recover known sensory pathways and finer motifs (e.g. fan-shaped-body layers) without only reproducing the atlas.
ocar.action: Kunin, Guo, Bassler, Pitkow, and Josić apply a machine-learning community-detection algorithm maximizing generalized modularity density to the Hemibrain (Journal of Neuroscience / catalog 2022), resolving communities from large to small scales.
ocar.resolution: The network is hierarchically organized: larger communities compose smaller ones. Methods recover known features including sensory pathways, automatically recover layered fan-shaped-body structure and finer up/downstream patterns, and find novel modular organization of the superior neuropil into pathway-like clusters. Fine-scale reconstruction is thus detailed enough to identify organization across scales and enable predictions about parts’ structure and function.
ocar.future_work: Predictions about superior neuropil pathways and finer FB connectivity are offered for functional tests.

summaries.beginner: A partial fly-brain wiring list with more than 20,000 cells was clustered into nested communities, from huge groups down to dozens of cells. The clusters recover known sensory paths and layered center-brain structure, and suggest new pathways in a less-charted region.
summaries.intermediate: Kunin et al. (Journal of Neuroscience 2022; bioRxiv DOI in catalog) detect communities in the Drosophila Hemibrain (>20,000 neurons, 10 million synapses) by maximizing generalized modularity density across scales. They report hierarchical modules, recovery of sensory pathways and fan-shaped-body layers (plus finer up/downstream structure), and a novel modular superior neuropil. They argue synapse-resolution graphs suffice to reveal multi-scale organization.
summaries.advanced: >20,000 neurons / 10 million synapses are Hemibrain figures as stated (partial brain). Novel superior neuropil modules are predictions. Automatic recovery of known FB layers is a sanity check plus refinement. DS05 hemibrain / fly / graph analysis match. Catalog venue Journal of Neuroscience with bioRxiv-style DOI in id—use shard journal/year.

plain_language_summary: A partial fly-brain wiring list with more than 20,000 cells was clustered into nested communities, from huge groups down to dozens of cells. The clusters recover known sensory paths and layered center-brain structure, and suggest new pathways in a less-charted region.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM images and dense segmentations are now petascale and growing, requiring mass production of neuron skeletons, multi-resolution meshes, image pyramids for visualization, and tools to manage the data. Open tools for large-scale meshing, skeletonization, and management had been missing.
ocar.challenge: Economical, horizontally scalable computation on cloud or cluster, for meshing, skeletonization, hierarchy creation, and data management, must be proven at this scale.
ocar.action: Kubota, Raghavan, Silversmith, Zlateski, Bae, Tartavull, Kemnitz, Wu, and Seung present Igneous in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022): a Python distributed-computing framework for meshing, skeletonization, image-hierarchy creation, and data management on cloud or cluster, proven to scale horizontally.
ocar.resolution: Igneous enables economical production of dense segmentation-derived meshes, skeletons, and visualization pyramids, with a sketched computing framework, usage, and characterization of performance and storage. It is positioned for petascale EM segmentation derivatives (CloudVolume/Igneous).
ocar.future_work: Continued horizontal scaling as volumes grow is the design goal; the paper characterizes current performance and storage.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored a petabyte-scale brain volume, someone still has to build the 3D surfaces, stick-figure skeletons, and zoom levels for viewing. This open Python system spreads that factory work across many machines.
summaries.intermediate: Kubota et al. in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022) introduce Igneous, a Python framework for distributed meshing, neuron skeletonization, hierarchical downsampling, and data management of dense 3D EM segmentations. It runs on cloud or cluster, scales horizontally, and is aimed at petascale visualization and analysis derivatives. Performance and storage are characterized.
summaries.advanced: This is infrastructure; no biological circuit result. Organism/dataset unspecified. CloudVolume/Igneous method tag matches. Horizontal scaling is claimed as proven, without numbers in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored a petabyte-scale brain volume, someone still has to build the 3D surfaces, stick-figure skeletons, and zoom levels for viewing. This open Python system spreads that factory work across many machines.

ocar.opportunity: Most brain studies focus on small circuits, but behavior engages many regions. Whole-brain recording at cellular resolution in small behaving animals (C. elegans, Drosophila, larval zebrafish) now captures sensory, decision, and motor circuits together—yet activity is mutually contingent on behavior, especially for navigation, mating, or hunting in freely moving animals.
ocar.challenge: Many signaling and feedback pathways exist only in freely moving animals. High-dimensional brain activity plus behavioral dynamics need new theoretical approaches; modeling is multiscale from synapses to brain areas.
ocar.action: Lin, Witvliet, Hernandez-Nunez, Linderman, Samuel, and Venkatachalam review in Nature Reviews Physics (2022) experimental and theoretical methods for whole-brain activity and behavior in worms, flies, and fish, including optical microscopy advances and the role of the connectome as a structural organizer of activity alongside molecular and non-synaptic mechanisms.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys how whole-brain cellular imaging during behavior is now feasible in these small animals, argues that behavior provides necessary context for brain-wide dynamics, and outlines top-down and bottom-up modeling strategies. Physics is invited to contribute to this systems-neuroscience field.
ocar.future_work: Integrating connectome, cellular properties, and behavioral state into models of brain-wide dynamics is the agenda they set.

summaries.beginner: We can now watch nearly every brain cell in a tiny moving worm, fly, or fish. This review explains why those movies only make sense together with what the animal is doing, and how wiring diagrams, cell chemistry, and behavior all shape the activity.
summaries.intermediate: Lin et al. in Nature Reviews Physics (2022) review whole-brain cellular-resolution imaging in behaving C. elegans, Drosophila, and larval zebrafish. They stress that activity and behavior are mutually contingent, especially in freely moving animals, and that connectome, synaptic/molecular properties, and non-synaptic state mechanisms jointly organize dynamics. Top-down (theory-first) and bottom-up (structure in high-dimensional activity) modeling are both endorsed.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Catalog DS01 and DS15 match worm and fish examples; fly is also in the abstract. No new dataset. “Complete understanding requires behavioral context” is the conceptual claim.

plain_language_summary: We can now watch nearly every brain cell in a tiny moving worm, fly, or fish. This review explains why those movies only make sense together with what the animal is doing, and how wiring diagrams, cell chemistry, and behavior all shape the activity.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomics needs automated reconstruction of both neurons and ultrastructure. Most methods treat cellular and subcellular structures independently; using biological connectivity consensus between them could improve agglomeration accuracy and efficiency and better match biological plausibility.
ocar.challenge: Independent agglomeration ignores that neuron and ultrastructure graphs should agree. A joint graph-partitioning model must reconstruct multiple structures in one optimization step and outperform hierarchical agglomeration on public datasets.
ocar.action: Hong, Liu, Zhai, Liu, Shen, Chen, Xie, and Han introduce a joint graph-partitioning model using connectivity consensus between cellular and subcellular structures (BMC Bioinformatics 2022) for neural-structure agglomeration.
ocar.resolution: The joint optimization reconstructs multiple structures in one step and outperforms existing hierarchical agglomeration algorithms on several public datasets. The intent is reconstruction goals more consistent with biological domain knowledge.
ocar.future_work: The idea is offered to inspire other reconstruction algorithms and biological data-analysis settings.

summaries.beginner: Computers usually glue together cell shapes and tiny internal parts as two separate puzzles. This method forces those puzzles to agree with each other, which the authors say makes the final wiring more accurate on public test sets.
summaries.intermediate: Hong et al. in BMC Bioinformatics (2022) propose joint graph partitioning of neurons and ultrastructure using connectivity consensus from biological domain knowledge. Multiple structures are reconstructed in one optimization. Experiments on several public datasets show improvement over hierarchical agglomeration methods.
summaries.advanced: Public datasets are unnamed in the abstract; improvement is not numeric here. “Biological plausible” consensus is a modeling assumption. Organism unspecified. Segmentation/infrastructure/graph-analysis tags match.

plain_language_summary: Computers usually glue together cell shapes and tiny internal parts as two separate puzzles. This method forces those puzzles to agree with each other, which the authors say makes the final wiring more accurate on public test sets.

ocar.opportunity: Fly EM connectomes are most useful when a neuron can be matched to light-microscopy driver lines so it can be targeted genetically. That typically requires finding a pair of lines whose overlap isolates the EM cell—hence fast morphological search across large LM and EM datasets.
ocar.challenge: Datasets differ in modality and scale. Researchers need an intuitive, rapid web application with an extensible data model, serverless architecture, and massively parallel image search, plus open APIs and processed data for reuse.
ocar.action: Clements, Goina, Hubbard, Kawase, Olbris, Otsuna, Svirskas, and Rokicki present NeuronBridge (bioRxiv/BMC catalog 2022): a web application for putative morphological matches between large neuron datasets imaged with different modalities, including GUI, serverless cloud architecture, and parallel image search.
ocar.resolution: NeuronBridge fills a critical gap in the Drosophila workflow and is used by hundreds of neuroscience researchers. Software, open APIs, and processed datasets are offered for integration and reuse, with the service at neuronbridge.janelia.org.
ocar.future_work: Extensible data and APIs are intended for continued dataset ingestion and community reuse.

summaries.beginner: A cell found in a fly electron-microscope map is hard to study unless you have a genetic switch that hits that cell. This website searches huge light-microscope and electron-microscope libraries for look-alike shapes so you can pick those switches.
summaries.intermediate: Clements et al. (bioRxiv 2022; BMC Bioinformatics DOI in catalog) introduce NeuronBridge, a web app for rapid putative morphological matches across large Drosophila confocal and EM neuron datasets. They describe a GUI, extensible data model, serverless cloud architecture, and massively parallel image search. They report use by hundreds of researchers, with open APIs and processed data at neuronbridge.janelia.org.
summaries.advanced: Matches are putative morphology, not proof of cell-type identity. “Hundreds of researchers” is a usage claim. Catalog year 2022 versus BMC 2024 DOI suffix—card uses shard year. Confocal / EM / fly / infrastructure tags match.

plain_language_summary: A cell found in a fly electron-microscope map is hard to study unless you have a genetic switch that hits that cell. This website searches huge light-microscope and electron-microscope libraries for look-alike shapes so you can pick those switches.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-resolution connectomes now exceed memory on consumer workstations, and tissue diversity plus dataset size drive comparative queries for recurring connectivity patterns and algorithm reuse. Existing tools work when graphs fit in memory or are locked to one dataset (e.g. neuPrint, FlyBrainLab); general larger-than-RAM, multi-store analysis was missing.
ocar.challenge: Researchers must query diverse, often >TB raw volumes’ derived graphs, reuse algorithms across datasets, and interface with community stores without each lab reinventing a warehouse.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Johnson, Wester, and Gray-Roncal present a software framework for comparative connectomics (bioRxiv 2022) including visualization, a web portal, a connectivity/annotation query engine, and interfaces to community tools: MossDB, Grand, GrandIso-Cloud, and Motif Studio, interoperating with neuPrint, Neo4j, Pandas, and NetworkX.
ocar.resolution: The suite is described as making connectomes easy to analyze even when larger-than-RAM and stored in disparate datastores, enabling tool/algorithm reuse, standardization, and discovery, including public motif queries across connectomes.
ocar.future_work: Standardization and reuse across more community datastores is the stated goal.

summaries.beginner: Some wiring diagrams are now bigger than a desktop computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This software toolkit is meant to query and compare those giant graphs anyway, including searching for repeating connection patterns.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. on bioRxiv (2022) describe a modular comparative-connectomics stack: visualization, a web portal, query engines, MossDB annotations, Grand and GrandIso-Cloud for larger-than-RAM graphs and motif queries, and Motif Studio, with adapters to neuPrint, Neo4j, Pandas, and NetworkX. The aim is algorithm reuse and queries across connectomes that no longer fit in RAM. Existing in-memory or single-dataset tools do not cover that regime.
summaries.advanced: This is a software-framework preprint, not a biological finding. Interoperability claims are architectural. neuPrint method tag matches one supported backend. Organism/dataset unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Some wiring diagrams are now bigger than a desktop computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This software toolkit is meant to query and compare those giant graphs anyway, including searching for repeating connection patterns.

ocar.opportunity: Ever larger volume-EM brain datasets increase demand for automated connectomic extraction. An open-source toolkit that infers dense synaptic connectivity, runs on local HPC or rented cloud, and supports complex anatomical queries on >10 million synapses would make those volumes analyzable.
ocar.challenge: Prior SyConn-style inference must scale to tens of millions of synapses, provide web visualization, and remain usable off-site without only one lab’s cluster.
ocar.action: Schubert, Dorkenwald, Januszewski, Klimesch, Svara, Mancu, Ahmad, Fee, Jain, and Kornfeld introduce SyConn2 in Nature Methods (2022), a machine-learning framework for inferring and analyzing connectomes in volume EM, tested on datasets with more than 10 million synapses (e.g. zebra finch), with a web visualization interface and cloud or on-site HPC deployment.
ocar.resolution: SyConn2 makes such data amenable to complex anatomical and connectivity queries, as an open-source successor for dense synaptic-connectivity inference from vEM, illustrated on songbird tissue.
ocar.future_work: Cloud/HPC deployment is meant to spread the tool beyond a single site; further datasets are the implied application.

summaries.beginner: Huge 3D electron-microscope stacks of brain are of little use until synapses and cell parts are labeled automatically. This open toolkit does that labeling, works on a lab cluster or rented cloud computers, and lets users ask anatomical questions of maps with more than 10 million contacts.
summaries.intermediate: Schubert et al. in Nature Methods (2022) present SyConn2, an open-source machine-learning framework for dense synaptic connectivity inference from volume EM, running on on-site high-performance computers or rented cloud. It was tested on connectomic datasets with more than 10 million synapses and includes web visualization. Complex anatomical and connectivity queries are supported, with zebra finch as an example tissue.
summaries.advanced: >10 million synapses is the tested scale, not a universal limit. Songbird/DS19 is the example, not the only possible input. This is software/methods, successor to SyConn 2017. Infrastructure/acquisition tags: acquisition is weakly related; the paper is inference/analysis. Organism tag “other” matches songbird.

plain_language_summary: Huge 3D electron-microscope stacks of brain are of little use until synapses and cell parts are labeled automatically. This open toolkit does that labeling, works on a lab cluster or rented cloud computers, and lets users ask anatomical questions of maps with more than 10 million contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping molecular identity of individual synapses is crucial for circuit reconstruction, but EM—despite nanoscale resolution—has practical limits, tedious tracing, and has been applied only to very small samples such as C. elegans, tadpole larvae, fruit fly brain, or tiny mammalian bits. Expansion microscopy plus fluorescence synaptic probes could yield optical connectomes at single-synapse resolution in larger samples, fully automated.
