ocar.challenge: Subdiffraction synapse size and high density make light microscopy hard without expansion. Probes must be stable, specific, and bright, and compatible with available ExM protocols across mice, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, covering postsynaptic scaffolds/receptors, presynaptic terminals/vesicles, and even snapshots of synaptic activity.
ocar.action: Sneve and Piatkevich review in Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience (2022) advanced fluorescence staining methods and molecular probes for synapses compatible with expansion microscopy, including genetically encoded probes in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, plus delivery vectors, experimental considerations, and limitations.
ocar.resolution: They argue ExM with multicolor neuronal and synaptic labeling offers unprecedented fully automated tracing and mapping of entire circuits, and they review current methods for applying these probes in ExM, appropriate vectors, and emerging tools.
ocar.future_work: Experimental considerations and limitations for each tool are addressed as a guide to adoption; emerging tools are pointed to as the frontier.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can see every contact but are slow and limited in size. Making tissue swell and then using glowing labels for contact points could let ordinary light microscopes map wiring—and the molecules at those contacts—in bigger pieces of brain.
summaries.intermediate: Sneve and Piatkevich in Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience (2022) review expansion-microscopy-compatible synaptic labels for an optical connectome at single-synapse resolution. They cover genetically encoded probes for postsynaptic scaffolds and receptors, presynaptic terminals and vesicles, and activity snapshots in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans. Delivery vectors, ExM compatibility, and limitations versus EM’s tracing burden are discussed.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective, not a completed optical connectome. “Fully automated mode” is a claimed capability of ExM-plus-labeling, not a demonstrated whole-mammalian-brain result. Catalog datasets (elegans, zebrafish, Ciona) reflect example organisms; Drosophila and mouse are also in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can see every contact but are slow and limited in size. Making tissue swell and then using glowing labels for contact points could let ordinary light microscopes map wiring—and the molecules at those contacts—in bigger pieces of brain.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can image large specimen volumes at the resolution needed for dense connectomes, but high-fidelity volume assembly—seamless 2D stitching then 3D alignment—must keep up with tens of terabytes per day. A modular, scalable, parallel pipeline operating on metadata and transforms (without rendering intermediate images) would match that throughput.
ocar.challenge: Stitching, automated quality control, 3D alignment, and rendering must run on distributed systems, be triggerable after raw-data transfer, support multiple channels and modalities (including array tomography), and adapt new algorithms without rewriting the workflow. Mouse visual cortex, including one cubic millimeter, and human brain samples are production targets.
ocar.action: Mahalingam, Torres, Kapner, Trautman, Fliss, Seshamani, Perlman, Young, Kinn, Buchanan, Takeno, Yin, Bumbarger, Gwinn, Nyhus, Lein, Smith, Reid, Khairy, Saalfeld, Collman, and da Costa present ASAP (bioRxiv 2021): an Assembly Stitching and Alignment Pipeline built on Render services used for adult Drosophila brain assembly, with a workflow engine, QC, alignment, and rendering, plus multi-channel capability.
ocar.resolution: ASAP has been used for continuous processing of several large-scale mouse visual cortex and human brain datasets, including one cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex. Operating on metadata/transforms avoids intermediate renders; modularity eases new algorithms. The pipeline also applies to fluorescence and multimodal array-tomography datasets.
ocar.future_work: The authors position ASAP for ongoing production stitching at acquisition pace; applying the same engine to additional modalities is already supported.

summaries.beginner: Photographing a cubic millimeter of brain creates a flood of overlapping snapshots every day. This software assembly line stitches and lines them up as fast as they arrive, without writing huge intermediate pictures, and has been used on mouse visual cortex and human samples.
summaries.intermediate: Mahalingam et al. on bioRxiv (2021) introduce ASAP, a modular distributed stitching and alignment pipeline on Render services (as used for adult Drosophila brain assembly). It stores image metadata and transforms in a database, skipping intermediate renders, with automated QC, 3D alignment, rendering, and a workflow engine triggered after data transfer. It processed several large mouse visual cortex and human datasets, including 1 mm³ mouse visual cortex, and supports multi-channel/array-tomography data.
summaries.advanced: Catalog organism tag is fly because of the Render/Drosophila heritage; production results named here are mouse visual cortex and human—this card follows the abstract. “One cubic millimeter” is a processed volume, not a completed connectome in this paper. DS13 MICrONS is consistent with mouse visual cortex. Alignment/infrastructure tags match.

plain_language_summary: Photographing a cubic millimeter of brain creates a flood of overlapping snapshots every day. This software assembly line stitches and lines them up as fast as they arrive, without writing huge intermediate pictures, and has been used on mouse visual cortex and human samples.
